tier1_survived.claim: Full text could not be retrieved: despite Unpaywall listing this article as CC-BY open access with best-OA URL https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdfdirect/10.1029/2019WR025138, Wiley returned HTTP 402 to every fetch attempt (landing page, /full, /pdfdirect), and pubs.usgs.gov / Semantic Scholar / ResearchGate returned 403 or empty. All claims below therefore derive from the verbatim publisher abstract (mirrored in the USGS Publications Warehouse metadata) and from the companion USGS data release (Worland, Knight & Asquith 2019, doi:10.5066/P92F1ROU), NOT from the results tables. No NSE, KGE, RMSE or bias figures from this paper could be verified; anyone relying on this angle should obtain the PDF through a library and read Figures/Tables directly.
tier1_survived.effectSize: none available — no numeric results extractable
corrections: The access-failure half of the claim is accurate and I reproduced it: Wiley returns 402 to WebFetch and 403 to curl on every route despite Unpaywall listing the article as CC-BY, and pubs.usgs.gov / ScienceBase-via-WebFetch / CORE return 403 while IA Scholar and EarthArXiv have nothing. But the conclusion drawn from it — "no numeric results extractable," "Reported effect size: none available," "Reported split protocol: not-applicable," and "obtain the PDF through a library" — is wrong. The companion USGS data release doi:10.5066/P92F1ROU is fully public (ScienceBase item 5cae0b6ce4b0c3b006549e61, reachable with a browser User-Agent) and ships observed plus all 16 method predictions for 270,322 site-days across the 74 gauges (37 Mobile-Tombigbee, 37 Galveston-Trinity, 2000-2009), so method-level skill is directly recomputable. Doing so gives median per-site NSE of 0.779 for the paper's multivariate Gaussian copula versus 0.657 for the best QPPQ variant and 0.565 for the best drainage-area-ratio variant. The protocol is leave-one-site-out donor-based estimation (donors = all sites except the target). Most importantly, reading sb_functions.R settles the transferability question without the PDF: the shipped "perfect information" configuration inverts through quantile(R[,i], ...), the target site's OWN empirical flow-duration curve, and uses empirical correlations computed from the target's own record. That configuration is the partially-gauged case and is therefore inapplicable to our deployment target of an arbitrary ungauged map pin with no local history. The truly ungauged variant needs kriged correlations plus neural-net-regionalized FDCs from a second data release (doi:10.5066/P9YGKZZV, 9,203 HUC12 pour points, southeastern US, 1950-2009) and its performance figures are genuinely absent from the archive. Practical upshot for the project: this paper should be dropped as a modeling angle on transferability grounds (daily streamflow not water-quality exceedance, southeastern US not tile-drained Iowa, requires a gauged concurrent donor and the target's own marginal), not left open as an unresolved retrieval failure. General lesson for the remaining research: when a publisher blocks a paper, resolve the companion USGS/ScienceBase data release DOI with curl plus a browser User-Agent before declaring the numbers unavailable.

Verdict: the claim's core assertion (full text unretrievable; all statements abstract-only; no numeric results verifiable) is CORRECT and independently reproduced. Two detail fixes: (1) the article byline is Worland, Steinschneider, Farmer, Asquith & Knight (5 authors, WRR 55(11):9378-9397) — "Worland, Knight & Asquith 2019" is the 3-author companion data release doi:10.5066/P92F1ROU, and the claim conflates them. (2) pubs.usgs.gov is not "403 or empty": the Pubs Warehouse API returns record 70215879 with the full abstract, but its ONLY content link is "Open Access Publisher Index Page" back to doi.org — USGS hosts no PDF, so that route is permanently dead rather than transiently blocked. Also add: OpenAlex lists exactly one OA location for this work (the Wiley pdfdirect URL), i.e. no repository mirror exists anywhere in the OA graph, and Wiley's block is a Cloudflare bot challenge (HTTP 403 with cf-mitigated: challenge on direct curl; 402 through the fetch proxy), not a licensing paywall — a human with a browser would likely get the CC-BY PDF, so "obtain via library/browser" remains the correct next step. Finally, flag that this angle should probably be dropped regardless: the method requires donor streamgages and an estimated FDC at the target, its own abstract concedes it is only "competitive albeit nondominating" in the truly-ungaged case, and it targets daily streamflow in Trinity/Mobile-Tombigbee — not nitrate exceedance at an arbitrary Iowa map pin with 22/85 sites gauged.

The claim is directionally correct (full text is genuinely unretrievable through free routes) but wrong in three details and too pessimistic in its conclusion:

1. STATUS CODES: not "402 to every fetch attempt." Only the markdown-proxy fetch of /pdfdirect returned 402; direct browser-UA requests to the landing page, /full, /epdf, /pdfdirect and /full-xml all returned 403 (Cloudflare). Wiley's TDM API returns 400 without a token. Operative conclusion (no access) is unchanged.

2. "Reported split protocol: not-applicable" is WRONG. The companion data release explicitly documents leave-one-out cross-validation across sites (LOOCV for kriged inter-site correlations), and the abstract's "ungaged" scenarios hold the target site out entirely. This is a spatially-held-out, leave-one-site-out design — i.e. protocol-comparable in kind to our LOFO 0.820, not protocol-unknown. Note however it is leave-one-SITE-out within two donor networks, not leave-one-region-out; both basins' donor networks are always present, so it is a weaker spatial test than our leave-one-basin-family-out.

3. "Anyone relying on this angle should obtain the PDF through a library" understates what is available. The full study is REPRODUCIBLE without the PDF: doi:10.5066/P92F1ROU ships the raw inputs (74 gages, daily streamflow 2000-2009), site coordinates/areas, the R scripts implementing all 16 estimation methods, AND dv_output.csv containing the predicted daily streamflow for all 16 methods. Any NSE/KGE/RMSE/bias table in the paper can be recomputed directly from observed-vs-predicted in that release. Public, free, no auth, USGS ScienceBase, public domain (USGS data release).

4. Author list is five (Worland, Steinschneider, Farmer, Asquith, Knight) for the paper; the data release has three (Worland, Knight, Asquith). Do not conflate them.

TRANSFERABILITY — must be stated prominently, and it kills this angle for our deployment target regardless of whether the PDF is ever read: every method benchmarked here is DONOR-BASED. Each requires (a) an estimated flow-duration curve at the target and (b) daily nonexceedance-probability time series from GAGED donor sites plus an estimated rank-correlation structure between target and donors. Our shipped product has neither a nitrate FDC nor a gaged nitrate donor network with known spatial correlation at an arbitrary map pin, and 61 of our 85 sites (all IWQIS) have zero discharge data. Two of the abstract's four headline claims — (1) "the limiting case of perfect information" and (3) "partially gaged sites with several years of available data" — require target-site observations and are therefore inapplicable by construction. The one scenario that matches our setting is the truly ungaged one, and the abstract's own wording there is a NEGATIVE/NULL result: copulas "remain a competitive albeit nondominating method for ungaged sites ... when realistic error is introduced in the estimation of FDCs and correlations." That is the honest, citable takeaway: at the ungaged end, the sophisticated method does not beat simpler baselines. Add domain distance: 74 streamgages in humid/subtropical southeastern basins (Mobile-Tombigbee, Trinity), daily STREAMFLOW, not water-quality exceedance in tile-drained Iowa row-crop basins. And the n=74 is 37+37 within two donor networks — the effective number of independent between-region units is 2, not 74 — so it offers no evidence that donor/copula machinery survives at our n=19 independent basin families.

tier1_survived.claim: The study's entire evidence base is 74 USGS streamgages — 37 in the Mobile-Tombigbee River Basin (HUC4 0316) and 37 in the Trinity River Basin (HUC4 1201-1204) — with a decade of daily streamflow (2000-2009), and it compares 16 distinct streamflow-estimation methods on that network. This is an unusually SMALL donor network for a regionalization paper (contrast CAMELS studies at 531-671 basins), which makes it one of the few QPPQ-family results whose sample size is within an order of magnitude of the Iowa project's 19 independent basin families. It is still ~4x more independent units than n=19, and the two basins are dense, spatially contiguous gauge networks — a condition the Iowa nitrate deployment (arbitrary map pin, no guaranteed monitored neighbor) does not satisfy.
corrections:
The claim is factually exact on every number (74 gages, 37 Mobile-Tombigbee HUC4 0316, 37 Trinity HUC4 1201-1204, daily 2000-2009, 16 methods, QPPQ/regionalization framing). Two characterizations need fixing, both of which strengthen rather than weaken the skepticism:

CORRECTION 1 - "~4x more independent units than n=19" is apples-to-oranges and directionally backwards. Iowa's 19 is a POST-COLLAPSE, leak-safe count derived from 85 raw sites (basins that nest and overlap in time are grouped). Worland's 74 is a RAW gage count with no equivalent deduplication. The correct raw-to-raw comparison is 74 vs 85 - Iowa is the LARGER network. Measured pairwise Spearman correlations (all 666 pairs per basin) show Mobile-Tombigbee median rho 0.774 with 42% of pairs above 0.8 and a max of 0.984, plus nested mainstem/tributary gage structure; applying Iowa's own nesting rule would collapse 74 to well below 19. Moreover the study fits and evaluates each basin SEPARATELY (model_e, model_w in sb_main.R), so the effective number of independent regionalization units is closer to 2, not 74. This paper is therefore NOT a demonstration that QPPQ-family regionalization works at small n; it is a two-basin study on dense, highly correlated networks.

CORRECTION 2 - the "spatial-holdout" protocol label is too generous, and the distinction is fatal for the Iowa deployment target. 7 of the 16 methods (QPPQ_nearest_neighbor, QPPQ_highest_rho, QPPQ_IDW, QPPQ_mu, bivar_cop_nn, bivar_cop_rho, multivar_norm_cop) use quantile(R[,i],...), i.e. the TARGET SITE'S OWN 10-year observed record, to build its flow-duration curve. That is the "partially gaged" half of the paper's title, not the ungaged half. In a genuinely ungaged application the FDC must be regionalized by a separate regression step that this data release does not perform - and that step is where most ungaged-basin error originates. Additionally, the default donor-selection step picks the highest-correlation donor using observed target correlations (leakage); the leak-safe variant requires the optional loo_krige_cor() kriging step that sb_main.R explicitly marks as not needed to run anything else.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE PROJECT: only 9 of 16 methods (DAR, IDW, correlation-weighted, and averaging variants) are genuinely ungaged-capable, and all 9 still require a gauged donor with a CONCURRENT time series. The Iowa product predicts at an arbitrary map pin with zero local history, has discharge at only 22 of 85 sites, ZERO of the 61 IWQIS sites, and no guaranteed monitored neighbor - so even the ungaged-capable subset has no donor to draw from at a typical pin. The target is also daily streamflow, not a water-quality exceedance probability. The claim's own closing caveat (dense contiguous networks, a condition Iowa does not satisfy) is correct and if anything understated. Treat this source as evidence about QPPQ's data requirements, not as a small-n existence proof.

The claim is factually exact but contains one framing error and one critical omission, both of which matter for how the Iowa project should use this source.

1. FRAMING ERROR — "74 independent units" is not apples-to-apples with Iowa's n=19, and overstates the donor network. The claim compares 74 raw gages against Iowa's 19 *leak-safe basin families* (85 raw sites collapsed by nesting + temporal overlap). Applying Iowa's own grouping rule to this network would collapse it far below 74: basin_area in coord_input.csv spans 15.72 to 47,698 (units per metadata: the abstract says squared meters but values are clearly km2), a ~3,000x range inside only two HUC4s. That range is the signature of heavy nesting — the large-area gages' basins physically contain most of the small ones. So "~4x more independent units than n=19" is an upper bound and probably a substantial overstatement; the effective independent count may be closer to Iowa's 19, or below it. This cuts IN FAVOR of the claim's own skeptical thrust: the source is even more sample-size-comparable to Iowa than stated, and correspondingly its results are even less able to certify a method at scale. It also means this study is itself vulnerable to pseudoreplication — 74 leave-one-out folds drawn from 2 contiguous basins are not 74 independent tests.

2. CRITICAL OMISSION — this is NOT an ungauged-prediction result in the sense the Iowa deployment requires. The paper title says "Ungaged and Partially Gaged," and the archived implementation is the partially-gaged case. In sb_functions.R the QPPQ variants are computed as `QPPQ_IDW <- quantile(R[,i], (U[,-i]%*%w)/sum(w))*area[i]` and `QPPQ_mu <- quantile(R[,i], apply(U[,-i],1,mean))*area[i]` — the `quantile(R[,i], ...)` term maps estimated non-exceedance probabilities back through THE TARGET SITE'S OWN OBSERVED runoff distribution, i.e. its own flow-duration curve. Likewise the rho-weighted and copula methods use `sigma[i,-i]`, the OBSERVED target-to-donor correlations. sb_main.R confirms this is the default and that removing the leak requires the separately-provided `loo_krige_cor` ("needed to use 'est cor' rather than observed"). Consequence for the deployment target: these 16 methods, as archived, require the target site's own observation record. Per the project's non-negotiable rule, that DOES NOT WORK for an arbitrary Iowa map pin with no local history. The claim should state this prominently rather than only noting the "no guaranteed monitored neighbor" issue — the deeper blocker is that QPPQ needs the target's own FDC, not just a nearby donor.

3. Minor corrections: the data file labels the second basin "Galveston-Trinity", not "Trinity" (metadata title uses "Trinity"). The archive's own sb_main.R carries a stale comment "estimate DVs using 11 models" while the output has 16 method columns — the metadata's 16, and the claim's 16, are correct. The claim should cite the paper DOI 10.1029/2019WR025138 alongside the data release. Finally, the target variable is daily streamflow, not a water-quality exceedance, so even the sample-size comparability does not make its effect sizes transferable to nitrate violation classification.

The claim is accurate on every checkable number - 74 gages (37 Mobile-Tombigbee HUC4 0316 + 37 Trinity HUC4 1201-1204), daily 2000-2009, 16 estimation methods - all verified verbatim in the ScienceBase metadata and independently confirmed in the data files (74 site rows, 16 method columns, 270,322 = 74 x 3,653 rows). Three refinements: (1) The split protocol is leave-one-gage-out on the DONOR side only. Verified in sb_functions.R: nearest neighbour, highest-rho donor, IDW weights, and the multivariate copula all exclude index i. But the archived sb_main.R still uses the target's OWN empirical FDC via quantile(R[,i], ...) and the target-inclusive empirical correlation matrix, i.e. the "partially gaged" configuration. The genuinely ungaged run requires separately executing loo_krige_cor for kriged correlations AND downloading modelled FDCs from the companion release. Describe it as "leave-one-gage-out donor exclusion; ungaged FDC requires an external regional model", not as a clean spatial holdout. (2) "The study's entire evidence base is 74 streamgages" is mildly overstated: the ungaged QPPQ variant depends on a companion multi-output neural network covering 9,203 HUC12 pour points across the southeastern US (DOI 10.5066/P9YGKZZV, Worland et al. 2019 WRR), trained on a much larger gage set. The 74 gages are the evaluation network for the 16-method bake-off, not the whole evidentiary footprint. (3) Drop "~4x more independent units than n=19". The 74 gages occupy only TWO HUC4 regions and are nested and strongly cross-correlated by design - inter-site correlation is the method's core input. Under the Iowa project's own leak-safe nesting rule these would collapse to far fewer than 74 families, plausibly comparable to or below 19. State "74 gages across 2 dense contiguous basins" and treat the effective independent-unit count as unresolved and likely much smaller. The claim's key qualitative point stands and should be kept: this is a small, dense, contiguous donor network, a precondition the arbitrary-map-pin Iowa deployment does not satisfy, and every one of the 16 methods needs a concurrent donor record - so for Iowa nitrate the donor pool would be the 22 discharge sites, with 0 of 61 IWQIS sites eligible as donors.

tier1_survived.claim: The QPPQ framework as defined by this paper explicitly decomposes the prediction into exactly the two pieces the Iowa project wants separated: (a) a flow-duration curve estimated at the ungaged/partially gaged target — the SITE LEVEL / marginal distribution — and (b) a time series of nonexceedance probabilities transferred from DONOR STREAMGAGE SITES — the TIMING / rank dynamics. The paper's stated contribution is a copula-based mathematical framework showing that prior FDC-based methods are special cases of a joint distribution whose rank-correlation structure across the gaging network is modeled separately from the marginals. DEPLOYMENT WARNING: component (b) requires at least one concurrently-observed donor site with an estimable rank correlation to the target; for the Iowa virtual-sensor product the analogous donor signal is the existing cross-site nitrate lag features (rest_of_state_nitrate_lag1/2/3/5), which already rank as the single most important feature — this paper is evidence that the correct architecture is to keep those as the timing channel and predict the target's marginal (concentration-duration curve) from static basin attributes as a separate output.
corrections:
The claim is directionally correct and the source is correctly attributed — the abstract states the FDC/donor decomposition almost verbatim — but three corrections are required before it is used to justify an architecture change.

(1) n IS WRONG. Not "74 basins." The study used 74 STREAMGAGES within TWO river basins in the southeast US, a decade of daily data. It is a dense nested donor network in two regions, not 74 independent catchments. The Iowa analogue (19 independent basin families, no dense donor network for nitrate) is a far sparser information regime than the one where the method was shown to win.

(2) "PRIOR METHODS ARE SPECIAL CASES" IS AN INFERENCE, NOT A QUOTE. The abstract says the framework "illustrate[s] the connection between copulas and prior FDC-based approaches." The special-case reading is almost certainly right on Sklar's-theorem grounds but was not confirmed against full text (publisher 402, no repository copy).

(3) THE PAPER'S OWN RESULT CONTRADICTS THE OPTIMISTIC USE OF IT. Verbatim finding (4): copula methods "remain a competitive albeit nondominating method for ungaged sites and partially gaged sites with limited data when realistic error is introduced in the estimation of FDCs and correlations across the gaging network." The measured advantage (finding 3) exists only for PARTIALLY GAGED sites with several years of their own observations. The Iowa deployment target — an arbitrary map pin with no local nitrate history — falls squarely in the regime where this paper reports NO dominance.

CORRECTED USABLE STATEMENT: Worland et al. (2019, WRR, 10.1029/2019WR025138; 74 gages, 2 southeastern US basins, decade of daily streamflow) provides a rigorous copula formalism for separating a site's marginal distribution from network rank dynamics, and is a defensible conceptual argument for a two-head architecture (static-attribute marginal head + cross-site timing channel). It provides NO empirical evidence that this architecture improves ungaged-site accuracy — its own ungaged-case result under realistic marginal-estimation error is explicit non-dominance — and no evidence at all for water-quality concentrations, tile-drained agricultural systems, exceedance classification, or n≈19 donor networks. Use it to justify an EXPERIMENT, never to predict a gain. And note the paper's implied warning: the architecture's accuracy is capped by how well the target's marginal can be regionalized, which is already the measured Iowa bottleneck (between_rate_r2 0.24), so the expected value of this refactor is low unless it is paired with genuinely new static predictors (tile-drainage density being the obvious missing one).

The claim's description of the cited paper is accurate and the paper is correctly identified (Worland et al. 2019, WRR 55(11), CC-BY) — the QPPQ marginal/dependence decomposition, the copula generalization of prior FDC methods, and n=74 are all confirmed against the publisher abstract. Four corrections:

1. "74 basins" is wrong: it is 74 STREAMGAGE SITES NESTED WITHIN TWO river basins in the southeast US, i.e. a dense clustered network, not 74 independent regions. This matters because the copula's advantage depends on estimating a pairwise rank-correlation surface across that dense network.

2. The claim omits the paper's own result for our exact regime. For UNGAGED sites with realistic error in both the FDCs and the network correlations, the abstract states copulas are "competitive albeit nondominating." The reported wins are in the perfect-information limiting case and at PARTIALLY GAGED sites with several years of local data — both of which require target-site observations or network density the Iowa product does not have. Cite the paper for the decomposition, never for an expected accuracy gain at an ungauged pin.

3. "QPPQ as defined by this paper" is a misattribution of provenance: QPPQ predates this paper (Fennessey 1994; Hughes & Smakhtin 1996; Archfield & Vogel 2010). Worland et al. GENERALIZE it via copulas; they do not define it.

4. The concluding inference — "this paper is evidence that the correct architecture is to keep rest_of_state_nitrate_lag* as the timing channel" — is unsupported and arguably backwards. A copula donor channel is site-specific and similarity-weighted; a single statewide scalar mean identical for every target pin is its degenerate collapse. Read properly, the paper suggests REPLACING the statewide mean with distance/attribute-weighted donor selection, not preserving it. Also note the decomposition ISOLATES rather than solves the project's deficit: it moves 100% of the residual error into the site marginal (the concentration-duration curve), which is exactly the between-site term the model already fails at (between_r2 0.21) and for which this paper supplies no estimation method. Finally, the paper's internal split protocol could not be verified (paywalled, no repository copy), so none of its numbers may be compared to our LOFO 0.820.

The paper attribution is accurate and n=74 is exact, so the claim stands as a description of the source. Three corrections to how it is being used:

(1) PROTOCOL: change "not-applicable" to "ungaged and partially-gaged scenario comparison, 74 sites in TWO southeastern U.S. river basins, ~10 years daily." Note the heavy nesting within two basins — effective independent units are far fewer than 74 — and note the paper's own ordering: the copula gain is largest for PARTIALLY GAGED sites with several years of local record and is only "competitive" for fully ungaged sites. Iowa's product is fully ungaged, i.e., the paper's weakest-advantage regime.

(2) THE DONOR MAPPING IS INCORRECT. rest_of_state_nitrate_lag1/2/3/5 is a statewide scalar mean, not a QPPQ donor. QPPQ's channel (b) requires per-donor concurrent observations plus an estimated rank correlation that decays with separation. To actually instantiate the paper's architecture, Iowa would need a distance-decaying nitrate rank-correlation model over the sensor network (a k-nearest-monitored-site nonexceedance transfer), which is a NEW feature the project does not have — not a restatement of the existing lag features. That is a testable, non-trivial proposal; the current lag features do not implement it.

(3) THE PAPER IS NOT EVIDENCE FOR THE RECOMMENDED ARCHITECTURE. It formalizes marginal/dependence separation; it does not evaluate two-headed ML architectures, does not address water quality, and does not solve the ungaged-marginal regionalization step — which is the entire Iowa deficit. Downgrade this from "evidence that the correct architecture is X" to "a conceptual/mathematical framing that motivates trying a separate concentration-duration-curve head, with the regionalization of that head still facing the unchanged n=19-families constraint."

tier1_survived.claim: Verbatim abstract finding, ranked qualitatively with no effect sizes given in the abstract: copula approaches (1) 'outperform other methods in the limiting case of perfect information with regard to the rank-based correlation structure and FDCs across the gaging network'; (2) 'provide a hedge against poor performance when donor information becomes sparser and less informative'; (3) 'outperform other methods when used for partially gaged sites with several years of available data'; and (4) 'remain a competitive albeit nondominating method for ungaged sites and partially gaged sites with limited data when realistic error is introduced in the estimation of FDCs and correlations across the gaging network.' Claim (4) is the falsifiable one that matters here: in the TRULY UNGAGED case with realistic FDC-estimation error, the sophisticated copula machinery is explicitly NOT dominant — it merely ties simpler methods. The authors' own framing therefore predicts that the copula/QPPQ upgrade buys little for a zero-observation target, and that the binding constraint is the accuracy of the regionalized duration curve itself, not the dependence model.
tier1_survived.effectSize: qualitative only ('outperform', 'competitive albeit nondominating'); no NSE/KGE/RMSE recoverable without the PDF
tier1_survived.splitProtocol: unknown — abstract does not state whether ungaged skill is leave-one-gage-out; the companion data release documents leave-one-out cross-validated site-to-site correlation kriging, which implies a spatial LOO design for at least the correlation component
corrections:
The claim is right in substance but imprecise in one inference. It states the paper's framing implies "the binding constraint is the accuracy of the regionalized duration curve itself, NOT the dependence model." The abstract does not support that dichotomy. Finding (4) attributes the loss of copula dominance to "realistic error ... in the estimation of FDCs AND correlations across the gaging network" — and the rank-based correlation structure IS the dependence model. Symmetrically, finding (1) grants copulas their win only under perfect information about BOTH FDCs AND correlations. So the authors name estimation error in the dependence structure as co-equal with FDC error in eroding the advantage; they do not isolate the FDC as the sole binding constraint.

Corrected statement: the paper's abstract shows that copula methods dominate only under perfect knowledge of BOTH the FDCs AND the inter-site rank-correlation structure, and degrade to merely competitive/nondominating for ungaged sites once realistic estimation error enters EITHER of those two inputs. The correct takeaway for this project is therefore slightly broader than the claim states — the limiting factor is the regionalization step as a whole (both the site's own level/duration curve and its estimated statistical relationship to the donor network), not the duration curve alone. This actually strengthens rather than weakens the claim's practical conclusion for our deployment target: at an arbitrary ungauged map pin we have realistic error in BOTH inputs simultaneously, i.e. we sit squarely in the regime the authors identify as the one where the sophisticated dependence machinery stops paying for itself.

Two secondary corrections: (a) n should be reported as "74 gages nested within only 2 southeast-US river basins," not "74 basins" — the effective independent-unit count is much smaller than 74, which is worth flagging under rule 5 since it means this evidence base is less of a large-n success story than the number implies; (b) the response variable is daily streamflow, not a water-quality exceedance, and this should be stated whenever the finding is cited in our context.

The claim is correct in substance - the abstract quote is exact, n=74 is exact, and finding (4) does say the copula approach is non-dominant for truly ungaged sites under realistic error. Three corrections: (1) The inference that "the binding constraint is the accuracy of the regionalized duration curve itself, not the dependence model" is the claim's own hypothesis and must NOT be attributed to "the authors' own framing" - the abstract introduces realistic error into the estimation of FDCs AND correlations across the gaging network jointly, and never decomposes which drives the collapse; because the rank-correlation field IS the copula's dependence model, the abstract is equally consistent with both legs being weak. Full text was inaccessible (Wiley 403 despite CC-BY), so no ablation isolating FDC error could be confirmed. (2) "The copula/QPPQ upgrade" conflates the method with its baseline: QPPQ is one of the prior FDC-based approaches the copula framework generalizes and is benchmarked against. Correct phrasing: for ungaged sites under realistic error, the copula machinery buys little OVER QPPQ-style baselines, with QPPQ among the competitive methods it ties. (3) The 74 sites sit within only TWO river basins, so the effective number of independent units is far below 74 - structurally the same collapse that reduces our 85 sites to 19 families. This strengthens rather than weakens the claim's skepticism, but should be stated rather than citing "74 basins" unqualified. Additionally, for our deployment target the relevant conclusion is stronger than the claim states: the entire QPPQ/copula family requires donor gages with concurrent observations plus an estimated duration curve at the target, so it is inapplicable at an arbitrary ungauged Iowa map pin regardless of its skill ranking, and its favorable findings (1)-(3) are all conditioned on local or high-quality donor information the product does not have.

Three detail corrections, none of which overturn the claim.

(a) "n basins: 74" should read "74 streamgages within TWO river basins" — nested, spatially dependent sites, not 74 independent catchments. This matters for the n=19 constraint: the study's evidence base is weaker than "74" implies, which cuts both ways (it is not a 500-basin CAMELS result that we must discount, but it also cannot support strong generalization).

(b) The claim's inference that "the binding constraint is the accuracy of the regionalized duration curve itself, not the dependence model" is NOT established by the abstract. Finding (4) introduces realistic error into "the estimation of FDCs AND correlations across the gaging network" — both components are degraded simultaneously, and the abstract does not decompose which one drives the loss of dominance. The dependence model at an ungaged site must itself be regionalized (the companion data release's kriged site-to-site correlations are precisely that), so correlation-estimation error is equally implicated. The defensible version: under realistic estimation error in BOTH the regionalized FDC and the regionalized rank-correlation structure, the copula advantage disappears; the abstract does not identify which of the two is binding.

(c) "Nondominating" is weaker than the claim's gloss "merely ties simpler methods." Nondominating means not uniformly best (e.g. not best across all sites, flow quantiles, or metrics); it is compatible with a modest average edge. Use the authors' word.

Operational bottom line for this project: the citation is legitimate and correctly quoted, but it is a streamflow paper whose ungaged result is qualitative, protocol-unstated, and drawn from nested gages in two humid southeastern river basins. It is adequate as a reason NOT to invest in copula/QPPQ machinery for the Iowa nitrate map-pin product; it is NOT adequate as evidence about what would fix the between-site term.

tier1_survived.claim: Performance is conditioned on an information-quality axis rather than reported as a single number: the paper distinguishes a 'limiting case of perfect information' about FDCs and rank correlations from the case where 'realistic error is introduced in the estimation of FDCs and correlations across the gaging network,' and reports that method ranking REVERSES between those regimes (copulas dominate under perfect information, are merely competitive under realistic error). Falsifiable implication for this project: any measured gain from a level/shape decomposition must be evaluated with the concentration-duration curve ESTIMATED FROM ATTRIBUTES under spatial holdout, never with the target site's observed CDC plugged in — the latter is the 'perfect information' regime and will overstate the gain, in the same way random splits over autocorrelated site-days overstate transfer.
corrections:
Correct the claim to: Worland et al. (2019, WRR, 10.1029/2019WR025138; 74 streamgage SITES within TWO river basins in the southeast US, one decade of daily streamflow) condition their results on an information-quality regime rather than reporting a single number. Copula methods "outperform other methods in the limiting case of perfect information with regard to the rank-based correlation structure and FDCs across the gaging network," but "remain a competitive albeit nondominating method for ungaged sites and partially gaged sites with limited data when realistic error is introduced in the estimation of FDCs and correlations across the gaging network."

The advantage DEGRADES TO PARITY; it does NOT reverse. No competing method is reported to overtake copulas, and the abstract separately reports that copulas "provide a hedge against poor performance when donor information becomes sparser," i.e. they are described as relatively more robust, not less, as information quality drops. Replace "ranking reverses" with "the copula advantage collapses from dominance to parity."

Two further corrections: (a) the "realistic error" regime is confounded with record availability — result (4) applies to ungaged AND limited-record partially gaged sites jointly, so it is not a clean single-axis information-quality manipulation; (b) the split protocol remains unverified (full text paywalled), so this paper's numbers must not be placed alongside our LOFO 0.820.

The falsifiable implication for this project survives and should be kept, with an added caveat: any measured gain from a level/shape (CDC) decomposition must be evaluated with the concentration-duration curve ESTIMATED FROM STATIC ATTRIBUTES under spatial holdout, never with the target site's observed CDC plugged in. Caveat: this is an analogy from streamflow FDCs to nitrate CDCs, not something the paper states. Also note that the copula/FDC machinery itself is largely inapplicable to our deployment target — its two strongest results (2 and 3) require the target site's own observations (partially gaged), which an arbitrary Iowa map pin does not have, and the framework requires a donor network of concurrently observed sites. Use this citation as support for the EVALUATION-PROTOCOL argument only, not as a recommendation to adopt copula/FDC transfer.

The claim is directionally correct and the cited source is real, correctly attributed, and quoted near-verbatim — but two details must be fixed before use:

1. REPLACE "method ranking REVERSES between those regimes" WITH "copulas lose their dominance between those regimes." The abstract's words are that copulas "outperform other methods in the limiting case of perfect information" but "remain a competitive albeit nondominating method ... when realistic error is introduced in the estimation of FDCs and correlations across the gaging network." Non-dominating is not the same as inferior; no reversal (crossover to another method being best) is asserted in the abstract, and the full text is paywalled (Wiley returns 402/403; Unpaywall lists no repository copy), so any reversal claim is unverifiable. Reported effect sizes: none recoverable — cite this as a direction/qualitative-regime result only.

2. RE-SCOPE THE AXIS. The paper's two regimes are about DONOR-NETWORK INFORMATION QUALITY (accuracy of the estimated FDC and of cross-site rank correlations), not about a train/test split protocol. The paper reports no split protocol and makes no leakage argument. The analogy to random-vs-spatial splits is the project's own inference, and it is a good one, but it should be attributed to the project rather than to Worland et al.

3. ADD THE n CAVEAT. n=74 gages but nested in only TWO southeastern U.S. river basins — the effective number of independent units is far below 74, the same pseudoreplication pathology as this project's 85-sites-to-19-families collapse. This weakens the paper as evidence that the method ranking generalizes, while strengthening the analogy for why our own numbers must be spatially held out.

4. KEEP THE OPERATIONAL IMPLICATION, ON ITS OWN LOGIC. "Any measured gain from a level/shape decomposition must be evaluated with the concentration-duration curve ESTIMATED FROM ATTRIBUTES under LOFO holdout, never with the target site's observed CDC plugged in" is correct and should be a hard rule for this project. It follows from the project's existing Rule 1 (spatial holdout only) plus the fact that a site's observed CDC encodes exactly the between-site absolute level the model is failing at — plugging it in would be handing the model the answer to the between_r2 = 0.21 problem. Worland et al. is supporting precedent that FDC-based literature conditions results on information quality; it is not the proof.

5. DO NOT IMPORT THE METHOD. Copula/FDC transfer requires a donor gauge with a concurrent record and an estimated cross-site rank-correlation matrix. It is a streamflow method, not a water-quality-exceedance method, and the partially-gaged variant requires the target site's own observations — disqualifying for the arbitrary-map-pin deployment target. At 19 independent families a network-wide rank-correlation structure is not identifiable.

The claim is directionally correct and its quotations are exact, but three refinements are needed.

(1) "RANKING REVERSES" IS AN OVERSTATEMENT — use "loses dominance." The abstract supports copulas moving from "outperform other methods" (perfect information) to "competitive albeit nondominating" (realistic error). That is a demotion from the top rank, not an inversion of the method ordering. Whether any competitor overtakes copulas, and by how much, is in the paywalled full text and was not verifiable. Restate as: "the paper reports that copulas' advantage is contingent on the information regime — dominant under perfect information about FDCs and rank correlations, non-dominant once realistic estimation error is introduced." This is the weaker claim, and it is fully supported.

(2) THE FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION IS AN ANALOGY THE PAPER NEVER MAKES, though it is a sound one. Worland et al. studied STREAMFLOW estimation via FDCs and the QPPQ family. They say nothing about nitrate, concentration-duration curves, exceedance classification, or level/shape decomposition for water quality. The extension from FDC to CDC is inference by structural analogy, not transferred evidence. It should be cited as methodological precedent for the general principle — that plugging in a quantity the deployed system would have to estimate creates an optimistic-bias regime — not as evidence that a CDC decomposition will behave the same way for nitrate. Notably, the project does not need this paper to justify the protocol rule: it follows directly from the project's own rule 1. The paper's value is that it is an empirical demonstration, in a neighboring domain, that the perfect-information regime does not merely inflate a number but changes which method appears best — which is a stronger and more useful point than "it overstates the gain."

(3) THE METHOD ITSELF IS NON-DEPLOYABLE HERE; ONLY THE CAUTION TRANSFERS. This must be stated prominently. Every method compared in the paper — copula and QPPQ alike — maps a time series of nonexceedance probabilities FROM DONOR STREAMGAGE SITES onto the target. That requires a correlated, concurrently-recording donor. The shipped product is an arbitrary Iowa map pin with no nitrate history and NO GUARANTEE OF A MONITORED NEIGHBOR, so the donor-transfer machinery does not apply. Further, abstract points (2) and (3) — the copulas' strongest results — concern PARTIALLY GAGED sites with several years of the target's own data. Those are categorically useless for this product and must not be cited as supporting evidence for it. Only point (1)-vs-(4), the information-regime contrast, is relevant.

ADDITIONAL TRANSFERABILITY CAVEATS. n=74 gages in two humid southeastern US basins; hydrology is unlike Iowa's artificially tile-drained agricultural systems, and the target variable is continuous streamflow rather than a binary exceedance at a 10 mg/L threshold. The n=19-independent-families constraint does not invalidate the protocol caution (a protocol rule is not sample-size-gated), but it does bear on the implication's practical use: with 19 effective units, an attribute-estimated CDC under spatial holdout will itself be noisy, and the gap between the perfect-information and realistic-error regimes should be expected to be LARGER here than in the paper's 74-site network, not smaller. That strengthens rather than weakens the recommendation. Recommended action stands: if a level/shape or CDC decomposition is trialled, report both regimes side by side — observed-CDC-plugged-in as a diagnostic ceiling only, clearly labelled as such, and attribute-estimated-CDC under LOFO as the only number comparable to the current AUC 0.820 / PR-AUC 0.634 baseline.

tier1_refuted.claim: The partially-gaged result — copulas 'outperform other methods when used for partially gaged sites with SEVERAL YEARS of available data' but are only 'competitive' for 'partially gaged sites with LIMITED data' — implies a data threshold on the order of years, not days, before target-site observations pay off. This is a direct negative for post-hoc site-level calibration / quantile mapping in the Iowa deployment: the shipped product has ZERO observations at an arbitrary map pin, which sits below even the 'limited data' regime where this paper already finds no advantage. Quantile mapping and site random-intercept correction are therefore usable only for the ~85 existing sensor sites or for future sites after multi-year monitoring, and must be stated as NOT usable for the arbitrary-pin product; the only estimable path for a zero-observation pin is predicting the duration-curve parameters from static basin attributes, which at n=19 independent families is a ~19-point regression.
why:
SOURCE IDENTIFIED AND CITATION IS ACCURATE. https://pubs.usgs.gov/publication/70215879 = Worland, S.C., Steinschneider, S., Farmer, W.H., Asquith, W.H., and Knight, R., 2019, "Copula theory as a generalized framework for flow-duration curve-based streamflow estimates in ungaged and partially gaged catchments," Water Resources Research 55(11):9378-9397, DOI 10.1029/2019WR025138, CC-BY. Retrieved via the USGS pubs-services JSON API (https://pubs.usgs.gov/pubs-services/publication/70215879) and cross-checked against the Semantic Scholar record; the two abstracts match character-for-character.

QUOTES ARE EXACT. Abstract verbatim: "...copula approaches: (1) outperform other methods in the limiting case of perfect information with regard to the rank-based correlation structure and FDCs across the gaging network; (2) provide a hedge against poor performance when donor information becomes sparser and less informative; (3) outperform other methods when used for partially gaged sites with several years of available data; and (4) remain a competitive albeit nondominating method for ungaged sites and partially gaged sites with limited data when realistic error is introduced in the estimation of FDCs and correlations across the gaging network." Study design per abstract: "a decade of daily streamflow data from 74 sites located within two river basins in the southeast United States." So n=74 and the phrasing in the claim are both correct.

THE CLAIM IS NEVERTHELESS REFUTED, ON FOUR GROUNDS.

(1) THE PAPER DOES NOT STUDY WHETHER TARGET-SITE OBSERVATIONS "PAY OFF." Points (3) and (4) are a ranking of copulas AGAINST OTHER FDC-BASED METHODS (QPPQ-family, nonlinear spatial interpolation of FDCs, etc.), all of which also consume whatever target-site record exists. The statement "copulas dominate at several years, only tie at limited data" is a statement about when the copula's RELATIVE edge over its competitors emerges. It is logically consistent with all methods gaining large absolute skill from a few weeks of target data. The claim converts a method-ranking result into a data-sufficiency threshold ("years, not days, before target-site observations pay off"). That inference is not supported by the abstract, and I could not obtain the body to check whether the paper reports absolute skill-vs-record-length curves.

(2) THE ZERO-OBSERVATION CASE IS NOT "BELOW EVEN THE LIMITED DATA REGIME" — IT IS ONE OF THE PAPER'S TWO HEADLINE REGIMES. Point (4) reads "for ungaged sites AND partially gaged sites with limited data." Fully ungaged (zero target observations) is explicitly inside the studied range, not outside it. The claim's central rhetorical move — that the Iowa deployment sits off the bottom of the paper's tested range — is contradicted by the sentence it quotes.

(3) "COMPETITIVE ALBEIT NONDOMINATING" IS NOT "NO ADVANTAGE," AND NOT A NEGATIVE RESULT. The paper's finding for ungaged sites is that the method performs on par with the best available alternatives under realistic FDC/correlation estimation error. That is a neutral-to-mildly-positive result for zero-observation regionalization, not "a direct negative." The claim upgrades "does not dominate" into "finds no advantage," which reverses the sign of the reported conclusion.

(4) THE PAPER IS ARGUABLY EVIDENCE FOR, NOT AGAINST, THE PATH THE CLAIM CALLS THE ONLY REMAINING OPTION. In the fully ungaged configuration, FDC-based estimation works exactly the way the claim's own final sentence describes: regionalize the FDC (the marginal, i.e. the absolute LEVEL) from static basin attributes, and borrow the nonexceedance-probability time series (the TIMING) from donor gauges. The abstract reports that configuration as competitive. So the source supports, rather than refutes, the static-attribute FDC-regionalization route for an ungaged pin. The claim's last clause is therefore right, but it is presented as a grudging residual when it is in fact the paper's own ungaged method.

FURTHER METHODOLOGY AND TRANSFERABILITY CAVEATS (these weaken the claim's evidentiary base rather than rescuing it):
- SPLIT PROTOCOL UNDETERMINED. The claim says "unknown"; I could not determine it either. Wiley returns HTTP 402/403 on the pdfdirect and landing URLs despite a CC-BY license; no repository copy exists (Unpaywall lists only the publisher location; EuropePMC hitCount 0; CORE has no match). Per rule 1, this must be stated as undetermined, and no number here is comparable to the project's LOFO 0.820.
- "SEVERAL YEARS" AND "LIMITED DATA" ARE NEVER QUANTIFIED IN ANY TEXT I COULD REACH. The claim's paraphrase "on the order of years, not days" is an unverifiable interpolation of an unquantified qualitative phrase.
- PSEUDOREPLICATION IN THE SOURCE'S OWN n. 74 sites inside only TWO river basins means heavy nesting and spatial dependence; the effective number of independent units is far below 74, likely closer to the project's own 19-family scale than the headline suggests. This cuts both ways: it makes the source less authoritative than n=74 implies, and it removes the usual "their n is huge, ours is 19" objection.
- DOMAIN MISMATCH. Daily STREAMFLOW in two humid southeastern basins, not daily-max nitrate exceedance in tile-drained Iowa row-crop basins. Streamflow has strong, slowly-decaying inter-site rank correlation, which is what makes donor-borrowed nonexceedance series work; nitrate concentration rank correlation between Iowa basins decays much faster and is driven by local N application and tile hydrology. Any transfer of the copula/QPPQ machinery to nitrate needs that assumption tested directly, and the project's existing cross-site donor feature (rest_of_state_nitrate_lag1, the top permutation-importance feature) is the closest existing analogue and does work.
- DONOR REQUIREMENT IS SATISFIED, NOT VIOLATED. FDC/copula methods need concurrent DONOR gauges, not target-site history. Iowa has ~85 nitrate sensors as donors. So the deployment constraint the claim invokes (zero observations at the pin) is not the binding constraint for this family of methods.
- DIRECTIONALLY, THE METHOD ADDRESSES THE PROJECT'S ACTUAL DEFICIT. The project is "a good timer, a mediocre site-ranker" (within_r2 0.42 vs between_r2 0.21). FDC-based methods decompose exactly along that seam: the marginal/FDC carries the absolute level (the failing term) and the copula carries the timing (the working term). Framing this paper as a reason not to pursue level correction is backwards.

WHAT SURVIVES. Only this much of the claim is supportable: post-hoc calibration that requires the TARGET SITE'S OWN observations (site random intercepts fit to local data, quantile mapping against a local empirical distribution) is unusable at an arbitrary pin — but that follows from the deployment definition, not from this paper, and the paper is not needed to establish it. Citing Worland et al. 2019 as the authority for it is a misattribution.

SOURCE VERIFIED, INFERENCE NOT.

Paper is real and correctly identified: Worland, Steinschneider, Farmer, Asquith, Knight (2019), "Copula Theory as a Generalized Framework for Flow-Duration Curve Based Streamflow Estimates in Ungaged and Partially Gaged Catchments," Water Resources Research 55(11):9378-9397, DOI 10.1029/2019WR025138, CC BY. Verbatim abstract retrieved independently from USGS pubs warehouse meta tags and from api.crossref.org.

Both quoted fragments are EXACT. Abstract points (3) and (4): "(3) outperform other methods when used for partially gaged sites with several years of available data; and (4) remain a competitive albeit nondominating method for ungaged sites and partially gaged sites with limited data when realistic error is introduced in the estimation of FDCs and correlations across the gaging network."

Where the claim breaks:

1. CATEGORY ERROR — between-method result read as a between-record-length result. Points (3) and (4) rank COPULA METHODS AGAINST OTHER FDC-BASED ESTIMATORS within fixed information regimes. Nothing in the abstract compares a site's accuracy at N days of record versus zero record. The pattern "copulas dominate at several years, merely competitive at limited data" is equally consistent with ALL methods improving monotonically with record length while their relative ordering converges. The claim's "implies a data threshold on the order of years, not days, before target-site observations pay off" does not follow from the cited text.

2. DROPPED CONDITIONAL. Point (4) attributes the loss of dominance to "when realistic error is introduced in the estimation of FDCs and correlations across the gaging network" — an injected-error condition, not record length alone. The claim omits this entirely, which is material because it is the stated cause of non-dominance.

3. MISREADING OF "NO ADVANTAGE." "Competitive albeit nondominating" means copulas perform about as well as alternatives — no advantage OF COPULAS OVER OTHER FDC METHODS. The claim converts this into "no advantage of having data." Different proposition, unsupported. Note also that the paper's UNGAGED branch is mildly POSITIVE ("remain a competitive... method for ungaged sites"), so the source is not a "direct negative" for the ungaged/regionalized path; if anything it endorses estimating FDCs at ungaged locations.

4. MISATTRIBUTED SUPPORT. The deployment conclusion — quantile mapping and site random-intercept correction cannot run at a pin with zero observations — is TRUE, but true by arithmetic (you cannot map quantiles from an empty sample). This paper is not the evidence for it, and citing it as a "direct negative" overstates what the source establishes.

5. n IS MISREPORTED, AND IN THE DIRECTION THAT MATTERS HERE. The claim reports "n basins: 74." The abstract says "74 sites located within TWO river basins in the southeast United States." Those are nested/overlapping gages inside two basins, so effective spatial independence is on the order of 2 regions, not 74 — likely pseudoreplication, and LOWER effective independence than Iowa's 19 families. This is the opposite of the CAMELS-scale concern; the study is small, not large.

6. TRANSFERABILITY GAPS UNFLAGGED. (a) Domain is daily STREAMFLOW in two humid SE US basins, not binary water-quality exceedance in tile-drained Iowa; FDC/copula machinery assumes a continuous flow variable with strong donor-target rank correlation. (b) The entire framework REQUIRES concurrent DONOR streamgage time series to supply the nonexceedance-probability series — a constraint the claim never mentions, and arguably more binding for the Iowa product than record length. Notably the project ALREADY has a donor-like signal (rest_of_state_nitrate_lag1 is the top permutation feature), so the donor half of the framework is partially available and the claim's framing obscures that.

7. PROTOCOL UNDETERMINED. The claim itself lists split protocol as "unknown," then draws a strong methodological conclusion from it. I could not retrieve the body either (Wiley Cloudflare 403 on pdfdirect/epdf/full; r.jina.ai returns the CAPTCHA interstitial; unpaywall lists only the blocked Wiley PDF; fatcat returned no archived copy; WebSearch budget exhausted at 200/200). Per rule 1, protocol is stated as undetermined, not guessed.

RESIDUAL UNCERTAINTY (why confidence is medium, not high): the full text may contain a record-length sweep that operationalizes "several years" numerically and could partially rescue the "years not days" reading. I verified only the abstract. The between-method vs between-record-length category error stands regardless, but the numeric threshold question is unresolved.

tier1_refuted.claim: Worland et al. (2019) trained multioutput neural networks (MNNs) on 688 USGS streamgages in the Southeastern US using 40 basin characteristics as predictors and 15 empirical flow-duration-curve (FDC) quantiles as simultaneous outputs, then applied the fitted model to predict FDCs at 9,203 ungaged HUC12 watershed pour points for six decades (1950-2009). This is a pure attribute-to-distribution regionalization: the entire predicted distribution at an ungaged location is a function of static basin attributes only, with no local observations required — structurally the same setup as predicting a nitrate concentration-duration curve for an arbitrary Iowa map pin from basin attributes. NOTE for our project: the evidence base is 688 gages; our n=19 independent basin families is ~36x smaller, and a 40-predictor -> 15-output neural network is almost certainly infeasible at n=19.
why:
PAPER IDENTITY CONFIRMED. Crossref + OpenAlex + Semantic Scholar on DOI 10.1029/2018WR024463 all resolve to: Worland, Steinschneider, Asquith, Knight, Wieczorek (2019), "Prediction and Inference of Flow Duration Curves Using Multioutput Neural Networks," Water Resources Research 55(8):6850-6868. Wiley full text is Cloudflare/402-blocked; no repository copy exists (OpenAlex `any_repository_has_fulltext: false`). I therefore verified against the AUTHORS' OWN CODE AND PROJECT DOCUMENTATION, which is primary and in some ways better than the paper text: GitHub `scworland/restore-2018` (the USGS RESTORE FY2018 project this paper came out of).

VERBATIM ABSTRACT (via OpenAlex inverted index) confirms only: "multioutput neural network models to predict flow-duration curves (FDCs) in 9,203 ungaged locations in the Southeastern United States for six decades between 1950 and 2009", combined loss enforcing "monotonically increasing quantiles", dropout for posterior-predictive distributions, and "test model performance under cross validation". The abstract contains NO gage count, NO predictor count, NO quantile count, and NO error metric.

REFUTATION 1 — THE SPLIT PROTOCOL IS NOT A SPATIAL HOLDOUT (decisive; this is the load-bearing error). `scripts/Worland/remake_scripts/keras_funs.R`, function `sw_k_foldcv`, lines 15-18:
    N <- nrow(data)
    set.seed(1)
    indices <- sample(1:N)
    folds <- cut(indices, breaks = k, labels = FALSE)
This is a RANDOM k=10 fold over ROWS of a site-decade table, with no grouping by `site_no`. Each gage contributes up to 6 decade-rows (1950-2000), and `build_mnn_quantile.R` returns results keyed `distinct(site_no, decade, variable)`. So the SAME GAGE appears in both training and test folds in different decades. That is textbook pseudoreplication / spatial leakage: the reported CV skill measures interpolation to a new DECADE at a LARGELY-SEEN GAGE, not transfer to an ungaged basin. The production model in `build_final_fdc_model.R` uses Keras `validation_split=0.1`, which takes the LAST 10% of rows — also non-spatial. The 9,203 HUC12 pour-point predictions in `predict_fdc_all.R` are pure unvalidated extrapolation; there is no held-out-ungaged evaluation anywhere in the workflow. Under our Rule 1 this number is NOT comparable to our LOFO 0.820, and the claim's "Reported split protocol: spatial-holdout" is simply false.

REFUTATION 2 — 27 QUANTILES, NOT 15. Both `build_mnn_quantile.R` and `build_final_fdc_model.R` define an explicit vector literally named `f27` with 27 entries (f0.02, f0.05, f0.1, f0.2, f0.5, f01, f02, f05, f10, f20, f25, f30, f40, f50, f60, f70, f75, f80, f90, f95, f98, f99, f99.5, f99.8, f99.9, f99.95, f99.98), and `loss_weights <- c(rep(1,10), rep(1e-2,17))` (10+17=27). `predict_fdc_all.R` confirms: `viol <- sum(yhat$viol)/(nrow(yhat) * 27)`.

REFUTATION 3 — ~956-962 GAGES, NOT 688. `data/FactsAboutSiteLists.txt` (project's own documentation): "there are 962 streamgages of the original 1,290 for which at least one complete decade of the six decades listed exists, and 2,816 decades are represented." I downloaded `scibase/gage/all_gage_covariates.csv`: 5,736 rows x 48 columns, 956 unique `site_no`, 6 unique `decade` (956 x 6 = 5,736 exactly). Note `combine_all_vars.R` already applies `drop_na()` before this file is written, so no further row loss. The effective modeling set is ~2,816 site-decades over ~950-962 gages. The figure 688 is unsourced and does not appear in any retrieved primary material.

REFUTATION 4 — NO EFFECT SIZE EXISTS. The claim itself concedes no NSE/RMSE/R2 could be retrieved, and I could not retrieve one either. Under Rule 2 the claim therefore carries zero actionable content: it cannot support any inference about how well attribute-to-distribution regionalization actually performs. "Design and counts" without a metric, where the counts are wrong and the protocol is misreported, is not usable evidence.

PARTIAL — "40 basin characteristics" is plausible but unconfirmed. The covariate table has 48 columns of which ~42 are basin attributes (minus comid/site_no/huc12/decade/lat/lon), and the model selects the contiguous block `select(d, major:flood_storage, -basin_area)`, whose exact width I cannot pin without the .feather. Caution: 40 is ALSO the width of the second hidden layer (`layer_dense(units = 40, activation="relu")`), a very plausible source of a garbled full-text-fragment read.

TRANSFERABILITY TO OUR PROJECT — fails on four counts:
(a) n. The real evidence base is ~956 gages / 2,816 site-decades, so our 19 independent basin families is ~50x smaller, not the 36x the claim states. The architecture (40 inputs -> dense 28 -> dropout 0.27 -> dense 40 -> dropout 0.70 -> 27 separate linear heads) has on the order of 2-3k parameters. Utterly infeasible at n=19.
(b) The paper provides NO evidence for the one thing the claim wants it for. Because CV was random over rows, the study never demonstrates ungaged-basin transfer. Citing it as support for "arbitrary Iowa map pin works" would import exactly the leaky protocol our CV design was built to avoid — the paper made the very mistake our 19-family grouping prevents.
(c) Target mismatch flatters the paper. Y is `log10((q + 0.001) / basin_area)`, i.e. area-normalized specific discharge. Basin area is a near-deterministic predictor of streamflow magnitude, so much of the apparent attribute-to-distribution skill is the area scaling baked into the response transform. Nitrate CONCENTRATION has no analogous normalizer; our between-site level problem has no free ride of this kind.
(d) The paper's own headline finding is a MILD NEGATIVE for this application: "basin characteristics are most useful for predicting smaller quantiles, whereas bias terms from neighboring quantiles are most informative for predicting higher quantiles." Static basin attributes were LEAST informative at the HIGH quantiles. Our target is a high-quantile exceedance (daily max >= 10 mg/L, top ~26%). So the study's own result argues that static attributes degrade precisely in the regime we care about.

SALVAGEABLE (worth passing on despite refutation): (1) The multioutput monotone-quantile architecture — one shared trunk, many quantile heads, joint loss enforcing monotonicity — is genuinely attribute-only and needs no local history, so it is structurally deployment-compatible even though it cannot be trained at n=19 in this form. (2) More actionable: the repo is a concrete free inventory of NHDPlus-accumulated static basin attributes we do NOT currently have and which speak directly to our between-site deficit — `bfi` (base-flow index), `twi` (topographic wetness index), `rdx`, `soller` (surficial geology), `aquifers`, `bedperm` (bedrock permeability), `hlr` (hydrologic landscape regions), `physio`, `ecol3`, `strm_dens` (stream density), `sinuosity`, `flood_storage`/`nid_storage` (dam storage). These are free from NHDPlus/EPA StreamCat, cover the full CONUS (so they handle our multi-state basin portions), and are static — matching our project's finding that the only wins came from geometry and static geography. That is a real lead, but it is a lead from the repo's attribute list, NOT support for the claim as written.

PAPER IDENTIFIED AND PARTIALLY CONFIRMED. Worland, S.C., Steinschneider, S., Asquith, W., Knight, R., Wieczorek, M. (2019), "Prediction and Inference of Flow Duration Curves Using Multioutput Neural Networks," Water Resources Research 55(8), 6850-6868, doi:10.1029/2018WR024463. Wiley full text is paywalled (HTTP 402 on /doi/full, 403 on /doi/pdfdirect and /doi/pdf even with a browser UA; USGS Pubs Warehouse 403; CORE 403). Verbatim abstract obtained from the Crossref API (api.crossref.org/works/10.1029/2018WR024463), and the authors' complete analysis code obtained from the public repo github.com/scworland/restore-2018 (this is the paper's repo: same authors, same "Southeastern United States" covariate data release, targets named mnn_quantile_est / snn_quantile_est / mnn_lmom_est in predict_fdc.yml).

CONFIRMED BY VERBATIM ABSTRACT: "We develop multioutput neural network models to predict flow-duration curves (FDCs) in 9,203 ungaged locations in the Southeastern United States for six decades between 1950 and 2009." Also confirmed: multiple response variables in the output layer corresponding to individual FDC quantiles; combined loss enforcing monotonicity; dropout for posterior-predictive distributions; LIME for interpretation; MNN beats single-output NN.

REFUTATION 1 - THE SPLIT PROTOCOL IS WRONG, AND THIS IS DISQUALIFYING UNDER RULE 1. The claim states "spatial-holdout". The abstract says only "test model performance under cross validation" - no spatial language. The authors' code is explicit: scripts/Worland/remake_scripts/keras_funs.R, function sw_k_foldcv, does `N <- nrow(data); set.seed(1); indices <- sample(1:N); folds <- cut(indices, breaks = k, labels = FALSE)`, called from build_mnn_quantile.R as `sw_k_foldcv(build_model, k=10, epochs=500, batch_size=100, ...)`. That is RANDOM 10-fold CV over ROWS, not over gages or regions. The rows are gage-DECADES: each gage contributes up to 6 rows (1950,1960,1970,1980,1990,2000) whose static basin characteristics are near-identical. Random row-wise folds therefore place the same gage's other decades in the training set - textbook pseudoreplication/level-memorization leakage, exactly the failure mode Rule 1 exists to catch. The identical random-fold code is repeated in dropout_runs.R for the uncertainty quantification. No leave-one-gage-out, leave-one-region-out, or PUB-protocol appears anywhere in the repo's neural-net path (a separate GAM path does produce all_gage_looest_*.feather leave-one-out files, but those are Asquith's L-moment GAMs, not the MNN). Conclusion: these numbers are NOT comparable to our LOFO 0.820. The claim's headline framing - "applied to 9,203 ungaged pour points" - describes the PREDICTION step, not the validation step, and the claim conflates the two.

REFUTATION 2 - "15 quantiles" IS WRONG FOR THE PUBLISHED MODEL. build_mnn_quantile.R and build_snn_quantile.R both use a 27-quantile vector f27 = f0.02, f0.05, f0.1, f0.2, f0.5, f01, f02, f05, f10, f20, f25, f30, f40, f50, f60, f70, f75, f80, f90, f95, f98, f99, f99.5, f99.8, f99.9, f99.95, f99.98, with `loss_weights <- c(rep(1,10), rep(1e-2,17))`. A 15-quantile vector exists ONLY in scripts/Worland/keras_training/cloudml/two_layer_keras_model.R, an early Google CloudML hyperparameter-tuning script (dated by its job IDs to June 2018) that uses plain `validation_split = 0.25` and is not the production model.

REFUTATION 3 - "688 streamgages" IS UNSUBSTANTIATED AND CONTRADICTED BY THE AUTHORS' OWN DATA RELEASE. I downloaded the released training tables: scibase/gage/all_gage_covariates.csv = 5,736 rows, 956 unique site_no, 949 unique comid, exactly 956 per decade x 6 decades. scibase/gage/all_gage_flow_stats.csv = 2,804 rows, 956 unique site_no (1950:363, 1960:485, 1970:484, 1980:453, 1990:455, 2000:564). The repo's data/FactsAboutSiteLists.txt independently states 1,290 screened gages overall and "962 streamgages" with complete 1950-2000 decades. Nothing yields 688. The effective training set is ~2,804 gage-decade rows from ~956 gages - which also means the model was fit on ~2,804 rows, not 688 units.

REFUTATION 4 - "40 basin characteristics" IS UNVERIFIED AND LOOKS LIKE A LIKELY TRANSCRIPTION ARTIFACT. The predictor block in code is `select(d, major:flood_storage, -basin_area)`; the released covariate file has 48 columns of which 44 are non-ID (comid, site_no, huc12, decade excluded), including categorical geology/ecoregion/physiography factors coerced with as.numeric(as.factor(.)). So "~40" is plausible in magnitude but I could not confirm the exact figure. Note that "40" also appears in the code as a HIDDEN-LAYER WIDTH (`layer_dense(units = 40)` in build_mnn_quantile.R; `flag_integer("dense_units1", 40, ...)` in the tuning script) - a plausible source for a garbled paraphrase.

REFUTATION 5 - THE CLAIM'S "NO EXACT ERROR METRIC" ADMISSION IS ITSELF GROUNDS FOR REFUSAL UNDER RULE 2. There is no NSE/RMSE/R2 to compare. The one quantitative-direction result recoverable from the verbatim abstract cuts AGAINST the claim's usefulness to us: "basin characteristics are most useful for predicting smaller quantiles, whereas bias terms from neighboring quantiles are most informative for predicting higher quantiles." That is a published NEGATIVE result for attribute-only regionalization of the UPPER TAIL: for high quantiles the LIME surrogates were dominated by the intercept/bias rather than by basin attributes, i.e. static attributes carried little information about the extreme end of the distribution. Our target - violation = daily max >= 10 mg/L at a 0.263 base rate - IS an upper-tail exceedance. The paper's own finding predicts that attribute-only prediction of our tail will be weakest exactly where we need it.

TRANSFERABILITY ASSESSMENT (independent of the above, all against the arbitrary-map-pin deployment target):
(a) The claim's structural analogy is HALF right. The MNN input side is genuinely attribute-only - no local observations, no gauged neighbor, no discharge at the target - so it does clear the deployment-target bar in principle, and NLDI is even used in the repo (nldi_funs.R). But the TARGET is a DECADAL flow-duration curve: one row per gage-decade, a 10-year aggregate distribution. It is not a daily time series and contains no timing. Mapped onto our decomposition, it addresses ONLY the between-site level term (our between_rate_r2 0.24 / between_r2 0.21), and provides no mechanism for the daily "when" that our model already does well. Adopting it means abandoning daily resolution, which the product requires.
(b) SAMPLE SIZE, RULE 5. Even accepting the smaller of the candidate counts, the evidence base is ~956 gages / ~2,804 independent-ish units. Our n=19 independent basin families is ~50x smaller than the gage count and ~150x smaller than the row count. A ~40-input, 2-hidden-layer (28 and 40 units), 27-output network is on the order of 2,500+ parameters; at n=19 effective units this is hopeless. The claim's own NOTE concedes this, which is to its credit, but conceding infeasibility does not make the cited evidence supportive - it makes the citation inert for our decision.
(c) DOMAIN. Southeastern US / Gulf RESTORE region: humid, forested-to-mixed, no artificial subsurface tile drainage. The covariate set (bfi, twi, rdx, soller surficial geology, statsgo, ecoregion, physiography, dams/flood_storage, NLCD classes, ppt/temp mean+sd) contains nothing analogous to tile drainage density or nitrogen surplus. Streamflow FDCs are also far more strongly attribute-controlled (area and precipitation alone explain most of the variance; note the code divides all quantiles by basin_area before log10, i.e. the dominant scaling is removed a priori) than nitrate concentration is. Transferring an "attributes predict the distribution" conclusion from unit-area streamflow to nitrate concentration is not supported by anything in this paper.
(d) DEPLOYMENT. Nothing here requires the target site's own observations - that part of the claim is accurate and is the claim's one genuinely useful content. But it is also the trivial part: our current model is already attribute-plus-weather with no local history.

BOTTOM LINE: the paper exists and 9,203 / six decades / 1950-2009 / multioutput-NN / attribute-only-input are correct, but the two numbers that would make it evidence for us are wrong or unverifiable (protocol is random row-wise 10-fold CV with same-gage leakage, NOT spatial holdout; 15 quantiles is actually 27; 688 gages is contradicted by the authors' released 956 gages / 2,804 gage-decades; 40 predictors unverified and possibly confused with a hidden-layer width), and there is no retrievable error metric of any kind. Under Rules 1, 2, and the stated default, this is refuted.

tier3_unverified.claim: Kamrath & Yuan (2023, J. Environ. Manage., DOI 10.1016/j.jenvman.2023.117598) partitioned daily loads by flow-duration-curve interval in 14 gauged Ohio watersheds (11 km2 to 16,388 km2, 2000-2020, min 3 years, water-quality sampling >=4 days/week from USGS-gauged sites). Across sites the MEDIAN fraction of annual load carried by the top 10% of flow days (m10%) was 58% for NO3-N, 66% for dissolved reactive phosphorus, 72% for total phosphorus, 77% for TSS; the top 40% of flows carried a median 93% of NO3-N export. This is a descriptive load-duration-curve (LDC) partition, NOT a predictive model, and every site required its own gauged daily discharge record.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: median m10% = 58% of annual NO3-N load in top 10% of flow days; top 40% of flows = 93% of NO3-N load (median); site range for top-40% NO3-N load = 54-98%
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 14 gauged watersheds (all Ohio, western Lake Erie + Mississippi basins)

tier3_unverified.claim: The paper's ONLY attempt to regionalize the load-duration curve from watershed attributes is a two-predictor multivariate linear regression: m10% (percent of annual load in the top 10% flow interval) = b0 + b1*log(watershed area km2) + b2*(percent agricultural land), fit on n=13 watersheds (Cuyahoga removed as an agricultural-land outlier), giving adjusted R2 = 0.86, F(2,10) = 37.7, p < 0.001, b1 = -4.24 (p<0.001), b2 = +1.1 (p<0.001). The equivalent model for the 10-40th percentile interval (m10-40) gave adjusted R2 = 0.71, F(2,10) = 15.8, p < 0.001.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: adj R2 = 0.86 (m10%), adj R2 = 0.71 (m10-40); log-area coefficient -4.24 percentage points per log-unit area, ag-land coefficient +1.1 percentage points per percent ag
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 13 watersheds in the regression (14 studied)

tier3_unverified.claim: The adj R2 = 0.86 attribute-to-duration-curve regression in Kamrath & Yuan (2023) was fit and reported IN-SAMPLE with NO cross-validation, no holdout, and no leave-one-watershed-out test, on n=13 basins with 2 predictors plus intercept (10 residual degrees of freedom). Therefore this number is NOT comparable to any spatially held-out skill estimate and provides no direct evidence that duration-curve shape transfers to an unmonitored basin.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: adj R2 = 0.86 reported in-sample only; 13 observations, 3 fitted parameters

tier3_unverified.claim: Kamrath & Yuan (2023) attempted NO prediction at ungauged or unmonitored sites: the analysis is restricted to watersheds with both a USGS daily-discharge gauge and a high-frequency nutrient-concentration record, and the paper contains no QPPQ-style flow-duration-curve transfer, no discussion of applying the relationships to unmonitored watersheds, and no explicit TMDL-practice application. The method as published cannot be executed at an arbitrary map pin with no discharge gauge.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: zero ungauged-site predictions; 0 of 14 sites tested without local discharge data

tier3_unverified.claim: The direction of the attribute effect in Kamrath & Yuan (2023) is that LARGER watersheds concentrate LESS of their load in high flows (log-area coefficient -4.24 on m10%) while MORE agricultural watersheds concentrate MORE (coefficient +1.1). This is a falsifiable, transferable hypothesis for a between-site level/shape term: basin area and percent-agriculture predict the SHAPE of a site's load-duration curve, and both attributes are already available in the Iowa feature set (log_basin_area, CDL crop fractions).
tier3_unverified.effectSize: b1 = -4.24 percentage points of annual load per log10-unit of area; b2 = +1.1 percentage points per 1% agricultural land

tier3_unverified.claim: Mann-Kendall testing in Kamrath & Yuan (2023) found NO significant positive or negative temporal trend in m40% (fraction of annual load carried by the top 40% of flows) at any of the study sites over 2000-2020, i.e. the flow-interval/nutrient-export partition was temporally stationary. This supports treating the duration-curve shape as a STATIC per-site property estimable from attributes rather than a time-varying quantity, but it was established only on gauged sites with 3-20+ years of local record.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 0 of 14 sites with a significant Mann-Kendall trend in m40% over 2000-2020

tier3_unverified.claim: In the Level 1 meta-analysis of 13 published studies on predicting flow duration curves at ungauged sites (10 usable, all leave-one-out cross-validated, 27 total method-results), the number of catchments per study ranged from 8 to 1080 with a MEDIAN OF 49, and the back-calculated Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency of FDC quantiles had 25% and 75% quantiles of 0.60 and 0.90 respectively. This is the closest thing in the chapter to a headline ungauged-basin skill number for regional duration-curve transfer.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: NSE of FDC quantiles: 25th pct 0.60, 75th pct 0.90 (interquartile range across 27 method-results)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 8 to 1080 per study, median 49; 13 studies, 10 used

tier3_unverified.claim: CRUCIAL NEGATIVE RESULT FOR THE ZERO-OBSERVATION DEPLOYMENT CASE: across the Level 1 assessment, estimating a site's long-term flow duration curve from a SHORT LOCAL RECORD at that site beat every regionalization-from-attributes method. Verbatim: 'predictions of long-term FDCs based upon 1, 2, 5 years of observed runoff all outperform any of the other methods' and 'predictions of long-term FDCs based upon five years of observed runoff largely outperform the best performing regional model, while one or two years of daily runoff are generally sufficient to obtain predictions of FDCs that are as accurate as the ones retrieved through regionalization' (Castellarin et al. 2004a resampling experiment). Implication: as little as ONE YEAR of local observation matches the entire regionalization apparatus, and the chapter explicitly warns 'it is generally not advisable to rely completely on any regional model, which should be used to provide a first order approximation of FDCs.'
