tier3_unverified.nBasins: unknown (Castellarin et al. 2004a resampling subset); 3 short-record results within the 10-study Level 1 set

tier3_unverified.claim: REGIONALIZATION SKILL SCALES WITH THE NUMBER OF GAUGED SITES IN THE POOL. Level 1 finding, stated as a main conclusion: 'The performance increases clearly with number of stream gauges in the region', with the trend 'particularly clear for the comparison ... for the intermediate classes of catchment number (from 20 to 250 catchments per study)'. The chapter concludes 'even if one is interested in estimating a FDC for a single catchment it may be worth basing the regionalisation on a large number of catchments.' In the Level 2 assessment the authors attribute the index method's poorer showing in Italy directly to 'the lower stream gauge density' there, versus Austria and France which 'both have a relatively dense stream gauge network'. This bears directly on the n=19-independent-basin-families constraint: the FDC literature's own evidence says n~20 sits at the BOTTOM of the range where performance is measurably degraded by pool size.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Monotone improvement across catchment-count strata; degradation clearly visible in the 20-250 catchment band; smallest vs largest strata differ clearly
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 27 method-results spanning 8 to 1080 catchments (Level 1); 1419 catchments pooled in Level 2

tier3_unverified.claim: THE LEVEL/SHAPE DECOMPOSITION IS EXPLICIT AND ASYMMETRIC IN DIFFICULTY. The index-flow framework models daily runoff as the product of two independent random variables: an index flow (mean or median annual runoff) carrying the site's absolute LEVEL, and a dimensionless duration curve carrying the SHAPE. Level 2 assessment quantifies the two halves separately over 1419 catchments, 4 method families, leave-one-out: 'R2 of the slope of the FDC were calculated for all methods in each study separately which gave a median of 0.26. Also the NSE of the quantiles of the scaled FDC were calculated which gave a median of 0.98.' I.e. the normalized SHAPE transfers almost perfectly (NSE 0.98) while the between-site SLOPE parameter is nearly unpredictable from attributes (R2 0.26) - a direct analogue of this project's within_r2 0.42 vs between_r2 0.21 split, and evidence that the between-site term is hard in the source literature too, not just here.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: median R2 = 0.26 for FDC slope (between-site shape parameter); median NSE = 0.98 for quantiles of the index-scaled FDC; indicative performance range 0.40-0.95 reported to Chapter 12
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 1419 catchments, 7 contributing author groups, 4 method families

tier3_unverified.claim: METHOD RANKING IS INCONSISTENT BETWEEN THE TWO ASSESSMENT LEVELS, AND THE AUTHORS ATTRIBUTE THE RANKING TO DATA DENSITY RATHER THAN METHOD QUALITY. Level 2 (1419 catchments, leave-one-out, ANE of FDC slope): 'overall, geostatistical methods perform best, followed by the regression methods' - but immediately caveated, 'This may be partly related to the higher stream gauge density of the data sets used for these methods.' Level 1 is contradictory: 'In both comparative studies, the regressions methods perform better than the index method, but when one considers all studies the index method performs better', and one of those head-to-head comparisons 'was only over two catchments'. Geostatistical performance 'strongly increase[s] with catchment area' because larger catchments overlap more with gauged ones. Process-based rainfall-runoff models underestimated FDC slope at both the smallest and largest catchments because they were calibrated on daily-NSE - 'the slope of the FDC was not captured well even in the calibration' - a direct warning that optimizing a timing-style loss does not deliver the distributional/level property you actually want.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Ranking: geostatistics > regression > index/process-based on ANE of FDC slope (Level 2); reversed in 2 of the Level 1 head-to-heads, one of which had n=2 catchments
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 1419 (Level 2); one cited head-to-head comparison used only 2 catchments

tier3_unverified.claim: HOW THE CURVE IS REGIONALIZED FROM ATTRIBUTES - the operational recipe, with named predictors. Three families: (a) QUANTILE REGRESSION on individual percentiles (no distributional assumption, but 'regressing a large number of runoff quantiles means a large number of multi-regression models' and 'may result in inconsistent estimates ... the estimate of Q(D1) may be smaller than the estimate of Q(D2)' - i.e. quantile crossing; Archfield 2009 / Archfield et al. 2010 use recursive regression to prevent this). (b) PARAMETRIC: fit a distribution per gauged site, then regress its parameters on attributes - Castellarin et al. (2007) used a 2-parameter logistic for the index flow and a 3-parameter kappa for dimensionless daily runoff, predicting the logistic position parameter (= mean annual runoff, the LEVEL) from area and mean annual net precipitation, the logistic scale from variability of annual net precipitation, and the kappa position (= within-year variability, the SHAPE) from catchment permeability and elevation range; cross-validation showed this beat parameter-regression models fitted to the long-term FDC alone. (c) RESCALED/POOLED: average the dimensionless FDC within a cluster of similar sites. Chapter summary of which attributes matter: 'Geology or geology/soil related indices and topographic elevation (in mountainous regions) are the most frequently used predictors of the slope/shape of FDCs, in addition to the aridity index, which governs the mean of the FDC.' Li et al. (2010, southeast Australia, lognormal FDC parameters regionalized) found catchment area and geographic location NOT sufficiently explanatory for FDC shape once specific (area-normalized) runoff and other covariates were used - a caution against this project's reliance on lat/lon as top-ranked features.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Li et al. (2010) index method beat linear regression, nearest-catchment, and hydrologic-similarity methods on within-catchment NSE of FDC quantiles (categories: NSE>0.75, 0.5-0.75, <0.5); exact per-method NSE values are in a figure, not the text
tier3_unverified.nBasins: unknown for Li et al. (2010) southeast Australia and Castellarin et al. (2007) northern Italy - counts not stated in chapter text

tier3_unverified.claim: In Worland et al. (2019), predicting each FDC quantile with an INDEPENDENT single-output neural network (SNN) produced 2,316 monotonicity violations (i.e., predicted quantile crossings where a lower exceedance quantile exceeded a higher one) after 400 training epochs, whereas the multioutput network with a combined loss across all 15 quantiles drove violations to zero for every cross-validation fold by roughly 100 epochs, and the SNN FDCs were 'generally less accurate' than the MNN FDCs. Falsifiable implication for us: fitting separate independent models per nitrate quantile/threshold will produce incoherent, crossing quantile predictions; a joint multioutput loss fixes this AND improves accuracy.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 2,316 monotonic violations (SNN, 400 epochs) vs 0 violations (MNN, ~100 epochs); accuracy advantage stated qualitatively only — no numeric RMSE/R2 delta retrievable behind paywall.

tier3_unverified.claim: Worland et al. (2019) report a quantile-dependent information split: static BASIN CHARACTERISTICS are most useful for predicting the SMALLER (low-flow) quantiles of the FDC, whereas the predicted values/bias terms of NEIGHBORING QUANTILES are the most informative predictors for the HIGHER quantiles. This is a direct, testable analogue of our level-vs-shape problem: it implies static attributes carry the anchoring/level information at one end of the distribution while cross-quantile structure carries the rest — i.e., a model should predict one anchor quantile from attributes and the remaining quantiles as offsets from it, rather than predicting every quantile independently from attributes.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Directional/interpretive finding from local surrogate models (LIME-style); no numeric importance values retrievable behind paywall.

tier3_unverified.claim: Worland et al. (2019) use neural-network DROPOUT AT PREDICTION TIME to generate posterior-predictive distributions for each ungaged FDC, i.e., they deliver a full uncertainty band on the regionalized duration curve rather than a point estimate. This is directly transferable to our deployment case (arbitrary map pin, zero local observations), where the honest product output is a predicted violation-probability distribution with uncertainty, not a single number — and it requires no target-site data.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Method described in abstract; no coverage/calibration statistics (e.g., 90% PI coverage) retrievable behind paywall.

tier3_unverified.claim: The Worland et al. (2019) framing has a hard limitation for our deployment target that must be stated: the paper regionalizes the TIME-AGGREGATED distribution (the flow-duration curve over a decade) at ungaged sites, NOT the daily time series. A duration curve tells you 'how high does this site get, and how often' but says nothing about WHICH DAY. Since our model is already 'a good timer' (within_r2 0.42, macro_auc 0.90) and a bad site-ranker (between_r2 0.21), the usable pattern is a two-stage decomposition — regionalize the site's nitrate exceedance-duration curve from static attributes, then use the existing daily model only to rank days within the site — but the source itself provides no evidence that such a coupling works for concentration or for water quality of any kind.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Scope limitation inferred from the paper's stated target (decadal FDC quantiles at 9,203 pour points); the paper does not attempt daily-series reconstruction (that is the separate QPPQ/copula line, e.g. Worland et al. 2019 WRR 10.1029/2019WR025138 on partially gaged catchments — which by name requires SOME target-site observations and therefore does NOT satisfy our zero-observation deployment case).

tier3_unverified.claim: A citing open-access source (Yi et al., HESS preprint hess-2024-355, 2025) benchmarks four models for 'ungauged' FDC prediction on 140 Korean streamflow stations and reports DNN beating RF, SVR and ENR by an average +0.90% R2 vs RF, +20.4% R2 vs SVR, +2.80% R2 vs ENR, with reported R2 values as high as 0.965-0.988 for individual quantiles. CAUTION: the train/test protocol is not stated as a spatial (leave-station-out) holdout anywhere in the text I could read, so these R2 values are NOT comparable to our LOFO 0.820 and should be treated as possibly interpolation rather than transfer. The same preprint also reports a negative result relevant to us: 'Different precipitation metrics had minimal impact on streamflow predictions' — i.e., varying accumulated-precipitation windows barely moved skill, echoing our own dead-last permutation importance for precip_in_1d and our failed rolling-precip ablation.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: DNN vs RF: +0.90% R2, -23.9% RMSE; DNN vs SVR: +20.4% R2, -395.5% RMSE (as printed); DNN vs ENR: +2.80% R2, -262.6% RMSE. Per-quantile R2 up to 0.965-0.988. Protocol undetermined — do not compare to LOFO numbers.
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 140 streamflow stations (Korea)

tier3_unverified.claim: EPA's load duration curve (LDC) framework is defined entirely on top of a FLOW duration curve at the site of interest: the guidance states 'loads are directly proportional to flows (i.e., load equals flow times concentration times a conversion factor)', and the loading capacity curve is produced by multiplying each flow-duration ordinate by the numeric water quality target. FALSIFIABLE/DEPLOYMENT-CRITICAL CONSEQUENCE: the method cannot produce a site-level concentration prediction without a daily discharge estimate at the target location. For the Iowa virtual-sensor product (arbitrary map pin, no gauge, discharge present at only 22 of 85 sites and 0 of 61 IWQIS sites), an LDC cannot be constructed from weather + land use alone; it would require first solving the ungauged-flow-regionalization problem. The document provides NO validated method or error estimate for doing so.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: No performance metric reported anywhere in the 74-page document; it is prescriptive guidance, not a validation study.
tier3_unverified.nBasins: not-applicable

tier3_unverified.claim: EPA's entire guidance on applying duration curves to UNGAUGED watersheds is two sentences with no quantitative support: 'Not all waters or watersheds have gaging stations or flow data available. In such cases estimation techniques are needed (USEPA, 2007). For instance, it may be appropriate to use flow data of a similar, representative water body to develop the duration curve, based on regression methods or drainage area ratios. The use of rainfall / runoff models can also be used to develop stream flow estimates for use in a duration curve analysis.' No accuracy, bias, or validation number is attached to drainage-area-ratio or regression transfer anywhere in the document. It further cautions that 'dealing with ungaged, headwater streams could present some obstacles in constructing a duration curve, as there is usually less data available on such waters.' NEGATIVE RESULT FOR THIS ANGLE: the standard US TMDL duration-curve literature does not supply a validated ungauged-transfer skill benchmark; it assumes the flow problem away.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: none reported
tier3_unverified.nBasins: unknown (no held-out basins; no validation performed)

tier3_unverified.claim: The only concrete, reproducible flow-regionalization protocol in the document is in the South Carolina DHEC Pee Dee River fecal coliform case study (Appendix A), and it is a purely GAUGE-TO-GAUGE index method: 'All flow data are first log-transformed to linearize the data because flow data are highly skewed. Linear regressions are then developed between 1) daily streamflow at the gage to be filled/extended; and 2) streamflow at all gages within 93 miles (150 kilometers) that have at least 300 daily flow measurements on matching dates. The station with the strongest flow relationship, as indicated by the highest correlation coefficient (r-squared value), is selected as the index gage... Flows will not be estimated based on regressions with r-squared values less than 0.25, even if that is the best regression.' The stated fallback when no coincident gauge exists is 'a watershed area ratio method derived by delineating subwatersheds, and relying on the Natural Resources Conservation Service runoff curve numbers and antecedent rainfall condition' using an upstream OR downstream gauge. FALSIFIABLE CONSTRAINTS: 150 km search radius, >=300 matched daily observations, r2>=0.25 acceptance floor. DEPLOYMENT LIMITATION: every branch of this priority list requires a gauge at, upstream of, or downstream of the target — which the Iowa map-pin product cannot guarantee.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Only the r2>=0.25 acceptance threshold is quantified; no out-of-sample flow error reported. r2=0.25 as an ACCEPTABLE index-gauge regression is itself a striking indicator of how weak this transfer is allowed to be in practice.
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: not-applicable (in-sample record-filling; no held-out evaluation reported)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: unknown — case study covers multiple SCDHEC 303(d)-listed water quality monitoring stations in the Pee Dee River basin; exact count not stated in the extracted narrative

tier3_unverified.claim: EPA defines a standard five-zone partition of the flow duration curve that functions as a discrete hydrologic-condition covariate: 'one representing high flows (0-10%), another for moist conditions (10-40%), one covering mid-range flows (40-60%), another for dry conditions (60-90%), and one representing low flows (90-100%)', with midpoints of the moist, mid-range and dry zones 'at the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles respectively (i.e., the quartiles)', the high zone 'centered at the 5th percentile' and the low zone 'centered at the 95th percentile'. The guidance explicitly states 'Other schemes can be used, depending on local hydrology'. RELEVANCE TO THE LEVEL/SHAPE DECOMPOSITION ANGLE: this is exactly a shape normalization — position on the site's own duration curve (a within-site relative coordinate, which the Iowa model already captures well as a 'good timer') is separated from the site's absolute flow magnitudes (the between-site level term, which is the actual deficit). The document offers the decomposition but not a way to predict the level term from basin attributes.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Zone boundaries: 0-10 / 10-40 / 40-60 / 60-90 / 90-100 percent exceedance; zone centers at the 5th, 25th, 50th, 75th, 95th percentiles.
tier3_unverified.nBasins: not-applicable

tier3_unverified.claim: EPA states an explicit applicability limitation that directly threatens the use of duration curves for Iowa nitrate: 'An underlying premise of the duration curve approach is correlation of water quality impairments to flow conditions. The duration curve alone does not consider specific fate and transport mechanisms, which may vary depending on watershed or pollutant characteristics. Such processes may include sediment attenuation, plant uptake of nutrients, chemical transformations, or bioaccumulation. Practitioners should consider using a separate analytical tool to develop a TMDL when factors other than flow significantly affect a water body's loading capacity.' It adds that the method 'is more appropriate in cases where flow is a primary driver in pollutant delivery mechanisms, and other processes are a relatively insignificant part of the total loading.' FALSIFIABLE PREDICTION FOR THIS PROJECT: because Iowa nitrate concentration is strongly modulated by N application/surplus, crop rotation, denitrification and tile-drainage routing — not flow alone — EPA's own criterion says a pure flow-duration framework is a partial tool for this pollutant. This is consistent with the project's finding that essentially all headroom is in a static between-site term rather than a flow/timing term.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Qualitative applicability criterion; no quantified degradation reported.
tier3_unverified.nBasins: not-applicable

tier3_unverified.claim: The document does apply the duration-curve framework to nitrate at exactly this project's threshold, but only as a deterministic target-times-flow calculation, not a predictive model: Figure 2-1 shows a 'Nitrate Loading Capacity Using Duration Curve Framework' with 'a sample calculation ... at one point along the curve corresponding to a flow duration interval of 60 using a nitrate target of 10 mg/L', and Appendix B Figure B-2 gives 'A loading capacity for nitrate in the Sangamon River ... using the drinking water maximum contaminant level (MCL) of 10 mg/L ... derived directly from the MCL (10 mg/L) and the duration curve using the flow to load calculation ... across the range of all daily average flows.' Data requirements are stated only loosely: 'While the number of observations required to develop a flow duration curve is not rigorously specified, a flow duration curve is usually based on more than 1 year of observations, and encompasses inter-annual and seasonal variations. Ideally, the drought and flood of record are included'; the SC case study used 'more than 5 years of water quality data (1990-2002)'. The case study also EXCLUDES the tails: 'The extreme high flow conditions (<10th percentile) and low flow conditions (>95 percentile) are not considered in development of these TMDLs' because of a 'stair step' effect from USGS rounding conventions. CONSEQUENCE: LDC practice discards precisely the high-flow tail where Iowa nitrate violations concentrate.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Nitrate target 10 mg/L (drinking-water MCL) — identical to this project's violation threshold. Minimum record: >1 year flow; case study used >5 years WQ data. Tails excluded: <10th and >95th percentile.
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 1 illustrative river per pollutant example (Sangamon River for nitrate; Portneuf River for phosphorus); no multi-basin validation

tier3_unverified.claim: CONTAINS NOTHING ON THE RESEARCH ANGLE — falsifiable negative about the source itself: this 11-page IAHS PUB position paper (Peters, Reynolds & Johnes 2007, IAHS Publ. 309, 63-73) contains ZERO mention of QPPQ, flow-duration curves, concentration-duration curves, load-duration curves, quantile mapping, quantile regression, hierarchical/Bayesian partial pooling, random effects, or domain adaptation. Its 21-item reference list is entirely empirical-regression, mass-balance and critical-loads literature (SPARROW, FAB, export coefficient models). Verified against the complete extracted text of the PDF. Anyone citing this paper as support for the level/shape-decomposition or duration-curve angle is citing it incorrectly.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 0 mentions of any duration-curve, quantile, or hierarchical-pooling method in full text
tier3_unverified.nBasins: not-applicable

tier3_unverified.claim: STRUCTURAL CLAIM DIRECTLY AGAINST A DAILY TARGET: the paper's central conclusion is that 'uncertainty of the estimates of average constituent concentration or yield decreases with increasing averaging time, e.g. a predicted annual flux is more precise than an instantaneous or daily flux', and closes with 'Although we may adequately predict average conditions (chronic), we may fail to predict biologically important extremes (acute).' This asserts that the DAILY-MAX, threshold-exceedance formulation is the hardest point on the aggregation curve, and that the ungauged-basin literature's reported skill is overwhelmingly for ANNUAL fluxes and is therefore NOT comparable to a daily-violation AUC. It also implies a testable, deployment-relevant fallback: predicting an annual or seasonal exceedance FREQUENCY per basin (a level/shape decomposition where the 'level' is a long-averaging-time quantity) should be materially more accurate than predicting individual site-days, and is worth measuring on the existing 19 families before more daily feature engineering.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: qualitative monotone claim: precision increases with averaging period; no numeric ratio given
tier3_unverified.nBasins: not-applicable

tier3_unverified.claim: THE CLOSEST PUBLISHED ANALOG TO THIS PROJECT'S EXACT TASK (attribute-only threshold-exceedance classification with no local history): Nolan, Hitt & Ruddy (2002, Environ. Sci. Technol. 36(10) 2138-2145, doi:10.1021/es0113854), as summarized here, fit a logistic regression for probability of nitrate contamination (>4 mg N/L) of recently recharged shallow groundwater across the conterminous USA, 'calibrated on 1280 observations, predicted the correct status of nitrate concentration in 75% of the 736 verification observations.' Six significant predictors: (1) N fertilizer loading, (2) % cropland-pasture, (3) ln(human population density), (4) % well-drained soils, (5) depth below land surface to the seasonally high water table, (6) presence/absence of unconsolidated sand and gravel aquifers. The paper explicitly partitions these: 'Predictors 4-6 relate to the hydrological pathway and time of travel, whereas predictors 1-3 relate to the source of the nitrate.' HALF the predictive variables are SUBSURFACE DRAINAGE-PATHWAY descriptors, none of which exist in the current 68-feature set — this is independent, quantitative support for prioritizing tile-drainage density / soil drainage class / depth-to-water-table over further weather features. Caveat: groundwater, not stream nitrate; 75% accuracy is against an unstated base rate and is NOT comparable to LOFO AUC 0.820.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 75% correct exceedance status on 736 held-out verification observations
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 1280 calibration observations, 736 verification observations (well/site counts, not basins); spatial independence of the verification set not stated in this summary

tier3_unverified.claim: NEGATIVE RESULT, n=88 SITES, LAND USE ALONE FAILS TO SET THE ABSOLUTE LEVEL: McLay et al. (2001, Environ. Pollut. 115(2) 191-204) assessed groundwater nitrate at 88 sites in New Zealand under mixed agricultural land use; per this paper, 'Although the authors documented the dominant land use and the local soils ability to leach nitrate, there were no discernible trends, and a risk assessment model was only able to explain 50% of the variance in the concentrations, with the permeability of the vadose zone being the most important parameter.' Associations only emerged for FINE-GRAINED operation types (dairy, drystock, drystock/sheep, market gardens, orchards) — market gardens highest, drystock/sheep lowest — not for coarse land-use class. This is a direct precedent for this project's between_r2 0.21 ceiling: coarse CDL crop fractions are the wrong granularity for between-site level, and a subsurface-permeability variable outranked all land-use variables. 50% of variance at n=88 sites also sets a realistic expectation ceiling for what n=19 independent families can support.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: R2 approximately 0.50 for site-level nitrate concentration; vadose-zone permeability the single most important parameter; no discernible trend from dominant land use
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: unknown (appears to be in-sample variance explained, not a spatial holdout)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 88 sites

tier3_unverified.claim: BENCHMARK FOR ATTRIBUTE-BASED N EXPORT, AND THE n=374 vs n=19 WARNING: 'six empirical and quasi-empirical nitrogen (N) watershed models were evaluated for predicting the riverine export of N from 16 large watersheds (475 to 70 000 km2) in the northeastern USA (Alexander et al., 2002); all models predicted the export to within 50% of the measured export. One of the models, SPARROW, was calibrated on 374 watersheds ranging in size from 10 to 2.9 x 10^6 km2.' So the ceiling for annual basin N export from source + runoff + land-use predictors is roughly plus/minus 50%, and the flagship method (SPARROW) required 374 calibration watersheds — approximately 20x this project's 19 independent basin families. Any recommendation to fit a SPARROW-style spatially-referenced source/attenuation regression here must be flagged as evidence-based at n=374, not n=19. Note also the aggregation mismatch: this plus/minus 50% is an ANNUAL LOAD figure, not a daily concentration, and is not comparable to LOFO R2 0.328.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: all six models within +/-50% of measured annual riverine N export
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: unknown for the 16-watershed evaluation (evaluation watersheds may overlap SPARROW's 374-watershed calibration set); not verifiable from this paper
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 16 watersheds for the model comparison; 374 watersheds for SPARROW calibration

tier3_unverified.claim: ORDER-OF-MAGNITUDE CEILING FOR REGRESSION-FROM-ATTRIBUTES, AND AN EXPLICIT DISAGGREGATION FIX FOR LARGE BASINS: 'The uncertainty in the prediction of annual major ion yields from basins ranging in size from 10 to 100 000 km2 in the USA, using a multiple linear regression model was an order of magnitude (Peters, 1984)', with predictors % rock types, annual precipitation, population density and average stream temperature; 'Precipitation quantity, a surrogate for runoff, and rock type were the most statistically significant predictors.' The paper attributes this failure specifically to basin size: 'in large basins the basic modelling unit cannot be the entire basin, but should be separate regions within the basin, which demonstrate distinct and different linear responses to the driving variables. Modelled separately with model estimates then lumped for the entire basin, a greater degree of the variance can be explained (Johnes & Butterfield, 2002).' This is a concrete, testable prescription for this project's largest multi-state basins (which are also the ones with the known crop/N-surplus under-count): predict per homogeneous sub-region and area-weight up, rather than feeding whole-basin lumped means to one model. Related documented scale failure in the same paper: catchment-attribute acid-sensitivity models gave 'reasonable predictions of sensitivity to acidification at a broad regional scale (>10 km2)' but 'the sensitivity prediction, particularly for high flow extremes, was poor for basin areas less than 10 ha due to fine scale, unmapped variations in bedrock geochemistry and land use' (Reynolds et al., 2001, Hydrol. Earth Syst. Sci. 5(1) 75-81) — i.e. attribute-based regionalization degrades at both ends of the scale range, and degrades WORST for extremes rather than means.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: annual major-ion yield precise only to one order of magnitude; Mg/Ca/HCO3 yields 4-10x higher from limestone than sandstone/granite basins
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: unknown (Peters 1984 multiple linear regression, calibration-set fit; no holdout described)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: unspecified count of US basins spanning 10 to 100,000 km2 (Peters 1984); Reynolds et al. 2001 catchment count not given in this paper

tier3_unverified.claim: Worland et al. (2019, WRR 55:9378-9397, DOI 10.1029/2019WR025138) benchmarked copula-based and QPPQ-based streamflow transfer on 74 USGS streamgages (37 in the Mobile-Tombigbee River Basin, 37 in the Trinity River Basin, southeast US) using 10 years of daily flow (2000-2009), under two explicit scenarios: 'ungaged' (target site has ZERO local observations, its flow-duration curve must be estimated from attributes/regionalization) and 'partially gaged' (target has a few years of local record). This is the canonical evaluation design for the level/shape decomposition question and it is done at a network size (74 sites, 2 regions) that is ~4x our 85 sites but far more than our 19 independent basin families.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: n/a — design claim
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (site treated as ungaged / partially gaged; exact held-out rotation not verifiable — Wiley full text returned HTTP 403, so protocol detail is from abstract + metadata only)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 74 streamgages (37 + 37 in two basins)

tier3_unverified.claim: The paper's own headline conclusion is that copula methods 'remain a competitive albeit nondominating method for ungaged sites and partially gaged sites with limited data when realistic error is introduced in the estimation of FDCs and correlations across the gaging network' — i.e. the sophisticated distributional machinery gives NO reliable advantage precisely in the zero-local-observation case. Its stated wins are (a) the limiting case of PERFECT information about the rank-correlation structure and FDCs across the network, and (b) partially gaged sites with SEVERAL YEARS of local data. Falsifiable implication for our deployment target (arbitrary map pin, zero nitrate history): duration-curve/copula transfer machinery should be expected to add little over simpler regionalization unless we can also improve the attribute-based estimate of the site's own duration curve.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Qualitative in the abstract: 'competitive albeit nondominating' at ungaged sites; outperforms at partially gaged sites with several years of data. Numeric magnitudes not retrievable (paywall/403).
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (ungaged scenario) and temporal-holdout-like (partially gaged scenario with limited years)

tier3_unverified.claim: The QPPQ framework the paper generalizes decomposes prediction into exactly the two pieces our project needs separated: (1) a TIMING/SHAPE component — a time series of nonexceedance probabilities p(t) taken from one or more DONOR gauges, and (2) a LEVEL component — the target site's own flow-duration curve (quantile function), which converts p(t) into physical units. Worland et al. state this explicitly: 'FDC-based streamflow estimation methods involve estimating an FDC at an ungaged or partially gaged location and using the time series of nonexceedance probabilities estimated from donor streamgage sites to generate estimates of streamflow.' This is a direct template for a nitrate analogue: our model already produces good within-site timing (within_r2 0.42, macro_auc 0.90) and could supply p(t), with a separately regionalized concentration-duration curve supplying the level (our weak between_r2 0.21 / between_rate_r2 0.24 term).
tier3_unverified.effectSize: n/a — method-structure claim

tier3_unverified.claim: QPPQ and its copula generalization REQUIRE at least one concurrently-observed donor gauge to supply the nonexceedance-probability time series; performance degrades as donor information becomes 'sparser and less informative' (the paper frames copulas as a 'hedge' against exactly that degradation, implying the baseline methods lose skill materially when donors are poor). For our deployment target this is a hard constraint: there is NO guaranteed monitored upstream neighbor at an arbitrary Iowa map pin. The nearest usable analogue in our existing feature set is the rest_of_state_nitrate_lag1 feature (already our top permutation-importance feature), which functions as a network-wide donor signal rather than a local donor — so the donor half of QPPQ is arguably already partly implemented, and the untouched half is the site-level duration curve.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Qualitative — degradation with donor sparsity described but not quantified in retrievable text.

tier3_unverified.claim: Within the paper's comparison, methods built on the QPPQ framework outperformed methods that did not use it, and the multivariate normal copula gave the highest log-NSE in BOTH basins, with a bivariate copula using the single most-correlated donor second best. However, in the Mobile-Tombigbee ungaged scenario the error components of the multivariate-normal-copula and the QPPQ-IDW (inverse-distance-weighted donor) methods were reported as 'almost identical', indicating little added benefit from working in z-space versus nonexceedance-probability space for low-to-medium flows. CAVEAT: these specifics come from search-result paraphrase of the full text, not from the verified article body (Wiley returned HTTP 403); exact log-NSE values were not obtainable.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Ranking only: multivariate normal copula > bivariate copula (most-correlated donor) > non-QPPQ methods on log-NSE; copula vs QPPQ-IDW 'almost identical' in the Mobile-Tombigbee ungaged case. Numeric values unverified.
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 74 (37 Mobile-Tombigbee, 37 Trinity)

tier3_unverified.claim: This paper is about STREAMFLOW only — it contains no water-quality, concentration-duration-curve, or load-duration-curve application. It therefore supports the level/shape decomposition as a framework but provides ZERO direct evidence that a concentration-duration curve for nitrate can be regionalized from basin attributes at ungaged sites, and it does not report how the FDC itself was regionalized from catchment attributes in a form retrievable from the open metadata (that step is the crux for us, since it is the analogue of our failing between-site term). Any transfer of this idea to Iowa nitrate must be treated as untested, and the regionalization step would be a regression of duration-curve quantiles on attributes fit over roughly 19 independent basin families — far below the 74-gage evidence base here and far below the 300+ catchment studies typical of this literature.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: n/a — scope/negative-coverage claim
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 74 (streamflow only; 0 water-quality sites)

tier3_unverified.claim: Kamrath & Yuan (2023, J. Environ. Manage. 336:117598) applied the flow-duration-curve / load-duration-curve framework to 14 Midwestern (Ohio, western Lake Erie and Mississippi basins) watersheds, 2000-2020, areas 11 km2 to 16,388 km2, minimum 3 years to 21 years of daily flow + nutrient monitoring per site. The paper is PURELY DESCRIPTIVE: it develops NO transfer model, NO regionalization of the duration curve from catchment attributes, and NO prediction for ungauged sites. It therefore does NOT provide QPPQ-style ungauged-basin skill evidence, contrary to what its title might suggest for this research angle.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: No predictive model fitted or validated; descriptive load partitioning only.
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 14 watersheds (13 used in regressions after excluding Cuyahoga as an outlier)

tier3_unverified.claim: Across 14 Ohio agricultural watersheds, days whose discharge falls in the upper 40% of the flow-duration curve accounted for 93% of NO3-N export (and 94% DRP, 95% TP, 98% TSS). Median fraction of load delivered in the top 10% of flow days alone was 58% for NO3-N (vs 66% DRP, 72% TP, 77% TSS). Implication for a nitrate violation model: essentially all load-relevant nitrate mass moves during the wettest 40% of days, so a duration-curve decomposition conditions almost entirely on the high-flow tail.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 93% of NO3-N export in upper 40% of flow days; 58% median in upper 10%.

tier3_unverified.claim: A two-predictor multivariate linear regression of the top-10%-flow NO3-N load fraction (m10%) on log(watershed area) and percent agricultural land use achieved adjusted R2 = 0.86, F(2,10) = 37.7, p < 0.001, n = 13 watersheds (coefficients: log-area beta = -4.24, p < 0.001; ag% beta = +1.1, p < 0.001). This is direct evidence that a BETWEEN-SITE nutrient-export property can be regressed on only two static basin attributes at a sample size (n = 13) comparable to this project's 19 independent basin families - but the R2 is an IN-SAMPLE adjusted R2 with no holdout or spatial cross-validation, so it is NOT comparable to the project's LOFO 0.820 AUC and is very likely optimistic at n = 13 with 2 predictors.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: adj R2 = 0.86, F(2,10) = 37.7, p < 0.001, n = 13; in-sample, no holdout.

tier3_unverified.claim: The same two static attributes (log watershed area, percent agricultural land) explained the moist-condition (10-40th percentile flow) load fraction with adjusted R2 = 0.71, F(2,10) = 15.8, p < 0.001, n = 13, and the combined upper-40% fraction with adjusted R2 = 0.71, F(2,10) = 15.8, p < 0.001, n = 13 (log-area beta = -1.27, p = 0.01; ag% beta = +0.46, p = 0.004). Sign structure is consistent and interpretable: larger basins concentrate LESS of their export in the highest flows, more agricultural land concentrates MORE. tier3_unverified.effectSize: adj R2 = 0.71 for both m10-40 and m40% regressions, n = 13, in-sample.

tier3_unverified.claim: The authors attribute the systematically LOWER top-10%-flow load fraction of DISSOLVED species (NO3-N, DRP) versus particulates (TP, TSS), and their higher moist-condition (10-40th percentile) fractions, to tile drainage: 'The greater m10-40 values for dissolved species were expected due to the widespread use of tile drainage in agricultural watersheds' and tile drainage 'allows a portion of the dissolved nutrient load to be leached out of wet soil during smaller precipitation events.' This is qualitative attribution across 14 watersheds with no tile-density covariate actually measured or entered into any model - it supports tile drainage as a hypothesized between-site control but provides NO quantitative effect size and NO usable tile dataset.

Using LDC operationally would require first predicting the FDC at the ungauged pin (a QPPQ-type step this paper does not perform), and 63 of the project's 85 sites - all 61 IWQIS sites - have no discharge data at all.

tier3_unverified.claim: In the Level 2 comparative assessment of this chapter — pooling 1419 catchments from 7 author groups, four regionalisation families (regression, index, geostatistics, process-based), all evaluated by leave-one-out cross-validation with each catchment treated as ungauged — the SHAPE of the flow duration curve was predicted far worse than the SCALED curve: 'R² of the slope of the FDC were calculated for all methods in each study separately which gave a median of 0.26. Also the NSE of the quantiles of the scaled FDC were calculated which gave a median of 0.98.' The slope was defined as (Q30% - Q70%)/40 in normalised runoff. The trend is particularly clear for the comparison of the pluses for the intermediate classes of catchment number (from 20 to 250 catchments per study)... These results suggest that even if one is interested in estimating a FDC for a single catchment it may be worth basing the regionalisation on a large number of catchments.' tier3_unverified.nBasins: Level 1: 10 studies binned by catchment count, bins spanning <20 to >250; Level 2: 1419 catchments

tier3_unverified.claim: CRUX WARNING FOR ZERO-OBSERVATION DEPLOYMENT: the chapter's single strongest quantitative finding is that a very short local record beats every regionalisation method. From resampling experiments in Castellarin et al. (2004a) comparing cross-validated regional FDCs (quantile regression, parametric, non-parametric) against empirical FDCs built from 1, 2 and 5 years of local observation: 'predictions of long-term FDCs based upon five years of observed runoff largely outperform the best performing regional model, while one or two years of daily runoff are generally sufficient to obtain predictions of FDCs that are as accurate as the ones retrieved through regionalization.' Confirmed in the Level 1 synthesis across all studies: 'Methods that use short runoff records at the site of interest perform better than any regionalisation method provided at least one year of daily runoff data is available, and significantly better if two to five years of data are available' — and in Figure 7.20 the short-record methods (3 results) sit above all 13 index-method and 11 regression-method results. IMPLICATION FOR THIS PROJECT: the entire duration-curve / level-shape angle delivers its gains from LOCAL DATA, which the arbitrary-map-pin deployment case does not have. Zero-observation regionalisation of the level is explicitly the weakest branch of this literature, not the strong one.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 1-2 years of local daily record ≈ best regional model; 5 years 'largely outperform' it; short-record group is the top group in Fig 7.20
tier3_unverified.nBasins: Level 1 comparison: 3 short-record results vs 13 index-method and 11 regression results; underlying Castellarin et al. (2004a) resampling study, n not stated in chapter

tier3_unverified.claim: HOW THE DURATION CURVE IS REGIONALISED FROM ATTRIBUTES — the chapter gives the operational recipe and the attributes that actually carry signal. Two-stage index-flow/parametric approach: fit a distribution to the normalised FDC at each gauged site, then regress its parameters on basin attributes. In Castellarin et al. (2007) the index flow is a 2-parameter logistic and the dimensionless daily runoff a 3-parameter kappa; 'They estimated the position parameter of the logistic distribution (which represents mean annual runoff) by regressions from area and mean annual net precipitation and, the scale parameter... from the variability of annual net precipitation. The position parameter of the kappa distribution (which represents the within-year variability) was estimated from catchment permeability and elevation range,' and cross-validation showed this outperforms traditional parameter regressions targeting only the long-term FDC. Li et al. (2010), regionalising lognormal FDC parameters across southeast Australia, found the position parameter positively correlated with mean annual precipitation and negatively with potential evaporation, the spread parameter tied to precipitation standard deviation and to leaf area index, and — notably — 'catchment area and geographic location does not appear sufficiently explanatory for the shape of the FDC.' The chapter's summary names the winning predictor set: 'Geology or geology/soil related indices and topographic elevation (in mountainous regions) are the most frequently used predictors of the slope/shape of FDCs, in addition to the aridity index, which governs the mean of the FDC.' RELEVANCE: the predictors that regionalise the LEVEL are subsurface/geologic (permeability, baseflow index) and long-term climatic — not the same-day weather scalars that dominate this project's failed temporal ablations; the chapter's baseflow-index result (Figure 7.11, 197 catchments, kappa shape parameter vs baseflow index) is the closest analogue to the missing tile-drainage control in Iowa.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Li et al. (2010) index method beats linear regression, nearest-catchment and hydrologic-similarity methods on within-catchment NSE of FDC quantiles (Fig 7.13, categories >0.75 / 0.5-0.75 / <0.5); no single scalar reported in the chapter
tier3_unverified.nBasins: Castellarin et al. (2007) central Italy, n not stated in chapter; Li et al. (2010) southeast Australia, n not stated; baseflow-index/shape relation shown for 197 catchments across the continental USA (Cheng et al. 2012)

tier3_unverified.claim: NEGATIVE RESULT ON THE WATER-QUALITY ANGLE: this chapter — the authoritative IAHS/PUB synthesis on predicting duration curves in ungauged basins — contains NO treatment of concentration-duration curves, load-duration curves, TMDL practice, or any water-quality constituent. The only water-quality touchpoint in the entire chapter is a single citation, Bonta & Cleland (2003), 'Incorporating Natural Variability, Uncertainty, and Risk Into Water Quality Evaluations Using Duration Curves,' JAWRA 39(6):1481-1496, doi:10.1111/j.1752-1688.2003.tb04433.x, cited only in passing alongside Vogel & Fennessey (1995) for the generic technique of combining an FDC with a rating curve to build a derived duration curve (the worked examples given are habitat-duration and power-duration curves, not concentration or load). SEPARATELY, the chapter never uses the term 'QPPQ'; Archfield (2009) and Archfield & Vogel (2010) are cited only for recursive regression to prevent quantile-crossing and for map-correlation reference-gauge selection, not as a named QPPQ method. CONCLUSION: the load-duration-curve literature is genuinely underused as claimed, but it is NOT covered by this canonical source and must be sourced separately (Bonta & Cleland 2003 is the entry point); and the chapter also reports zero hierarchical/Bayesian mixed-model or random-intercept regionalisation, and zero quantile-regression-forest / distributional-GBDT work — the regionalisation toolkit reviewed is entirely regression, index-flow, geostatistical (Topkriging / PSBI) and process-based.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 1 water-quality citation in ~90 references; 0 occurrences of 'QPPQ', 'load duration', 'TMDL', 'concentration duration', 'hierarchical Bayes', 'random effect', 'quantile regression forest'

EPA's own worked nutrient example (Figure B-2, Sangamon River) builds a nitrate loading-capacity curve using the drinking-water MCL of 10 mg/L — the identical threshold to this project's `violation` definition — 'derived directly from the MCL (10 mg/L) and the duration curve ... across the range of all daily average flows'. However, the document is agency guidance, not a study: it reports NO predictive skill statistics, no validation, no cross-validation, and no error bars anywhere in its 74 pages.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: none reported — zero quantitative skill metrics in the document
tier3_unverified.nBasins: not-applicable (guidance document; illustrative single-site figures only)

In such cases estimation techniques are needed (USEPA, 2007). For instance, it may be appropriate to use flow data of a similar, representative water body to develop the duration curve, based on regression methods or drainage area ratios. The use of rainfall / runoff models can also be used to develop stream flow estimates for use in a duration curve analysis.' The document further warns that 'dealing with ungaged, headwater streams could present some obstacles in constructing a duration curve, as there is usually less data available on such waters.' This means the standard US TMDL practice for the exact deployment case (arbitrary ungauged pin) is drainage-area-ratio transfer, with no published error characterization in this source — regionalization skill must be sourced elsewhere.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: no accuracy or transfer-error statistics reported for drainage-area ratio, regression, or rainfall-runoff FDC estimation
tier3_unverified.nBasins: unknown

tier3_unverified.claim: The Appendix A South Carolina (Pee Dee River Basin, SCDHEC) fecal coliform case study specifies an operational index-gauge regression protocol for estimating flow at unmonitored water-quality stations, with an explicit numerical rejection threshold: all flow data are log-transformed to linearize; linear regressions are built between daily streamflow at the station to be filled/extended and streamflow at 'all gages within 93 miles (150 kilometers) that have at least 300 daily flow measurements on matching dates'; the gauge with the highest r-squared is chosen as the index gauge; and 'Flows will not be estimated based on regressions with r-squared values less than 0.25, even if that is the best regression.' Remaining gaps are filled from successively weaker index gauges. CRITICAL LIMITATION FOR THIS PROJECT: this method requires a donor gauge with concurrent record; where no coincident gauge exists it falls back to a 'watershed area ratio method derived by delineating subwatersheds, and relying on the Natural Resources Conservation Service runoff curve numbers and antecedent rainfall condition' — i.e. it still presumes an upstream or downstream gauge on the same network. Only the drainage-area-ratio / curve-number variant is usable at an arbitrary Iowa map pin with no gauged neighbor.

tier3_unverified.claim: The canonical duration-curve binning is five fixed exceedance-percentile zones — high flows 0-10%, moist conditions 10-40%, mid-range 40-60%, dry conditions 60-90%, low flows 90-100% (Table 4-1, attributed to Cleland 2003) — chosen so that 'the midpoints of the moist, mid-range, and dry zones [are] at the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles respectively (i.e., the quartiles). The high zone is centered at the 5th percentile, while the low zone is centered at the 95th percentile.' EPA states other schemes can be used depending on local hydrology, citing an arid Southwest stream with zero flow more than half the time where 'two, three, or four zones' may be preferable. This is directly testable as a discretization for a site-conditional model: bin site-days by a regionalized flow (or precipitation-runoff) percentile rather than by raw weather scalars, which is a coarse (5-bin) shape representation that could be transferred with far fewer effective degrees of freedom than 68 features — relevant given the n=19 independent basin families constraint.

tier3_unverified.claim: EPA asserts a falsifiable diagnostic signature: the flow-percentile location of criterion exceedances discriminates pollutant source type. 'Impairments observed in the low flow zone typically indicate the influence of point sources, while those further left [high-flow zone] generally reflect potential nonpoint source contributions.' Table 4-1 formalizes this, rating point sources as High importance only in the low-flow zone and Medium in dry, while 'Storm water: Upland' is High in high/moist/mid-range zones and bank erosion High only at high flow. A supporting hydrograph-separation example (LaPlatte River, Figure 4-1) reports that surface runoff has 'its greatest effect during high flow conditions (median value of 61 percent)' of total streamflow. For Iowa row-crop nitrate — an upland nonpoint, tile-mediated source — this predicts violations should concentrate in the high/moist zones (0-40% exceedance), and the exceedance-vs-flow-percentile signature could serve as an unsupervised, transferable site descriptor. NOTE: EPA presents this as expert heuristic, with no statistics or classification accuracy given.

tier3_unverified.nBasins: not-applicable (one illustrative gauge, LaPlatte River, for the 61% storm-flow figure)

tier3_unverified.claim: EPA states explicit scope limits that constrain the LDC framework's applicability to nitrate specifically. Section 3a: 'The duration curve alone does not consider specific fate and transport mechanisms, which may vary depending on watershed or pollutant characteristics. Such processes may include sediment attenuation, plant uptake of nutrients, or chemical transformations.' It concludes 'The duration curve is more appropriate in cases where flow is a primary driver in pollutant delivery mechanisms, and other processes are a relatively insignificant part of the total loading', and 'Practitioners should consider using a separate analytical tool ... when factors other than flow significantly affect a water body's loading capacity.' Additionally, the SC case study excludes the tails from TMDL development: 'The extreme high flow conditions (<10th percentile) and low flow conditions (>95 percentile) are not considered in development of these TMDLs.' This is a NEGATIVE result of direct relevance: nitrate is subject to plant uptake and denitrification (the named exclusions), so a pure flow-percentile mapping is expected by EPA itself to be an incomplete predictor of nitrate concentration — consistent with this project's finding that a fixed weather-to-nitrate mapping fails to transfer the absolute level across basins. EPA also cautions the approach 'may not work in situations involving lakes or large coastal embayments'.

This is an independent, peer-reviewed statement that tile drainage controls the flow-interval distribution of dissolved N export — supporting the project's existing identification of tile-drainage density as the missing dominant between-site control. This makes an exceedance of the LDC mathematically identical to concentration >= 10 mg/L - i.e. the LDC adds no information beyond the concentration threshold when the target is flow-invariant, and its value is purely diagnostic (WHICH flow zone the exceedances fall in), not predictive.

tier3_unverified.claim: The guidance states two conditions that bound when a duration-curve framework is valid, both directly relevant to nitrate in tile-drained Iowa: (1) 'The duration curve alone does not consider specific fate and transport mechanisms... Such processes may include sediment attenuation, plant uptake of nutrients, or chemical transformations' and 'The duration curve is more appropriate in cases where flow is a primary driver in pollutant delivery mechanisms, and other processes are a relatively insignificant part of the total loading' (p.11, Section 3a); (2) on record length, 'While the number of observations required to develop a flow duration curve is not rigorously specified, a flow duration curve is usually based on more than 1 year of observations, and encompasses inter-annual and seasonal variations. Ideally, the drought and flood of record are included' (p.21). In the SC case study, 'The extreme high flow conditions (<10th percentile) and low flow conditions (>95 percentile) are not considered in development of these TMDLs' (p.21), and seasonal variation was addressed by 'using more than 5 years of water quality' data (Section 5.5). Interpretation flag: because nitrate is strongly modulated by plant uptake and denitrification, EPA's own criterion for LDC appropriateness (flow as the dominant driver, other processes insignificant) is the assumption most at risk for this application.
